Ignition key icon (available for the “Idle” field) — determines whether the ignition state is taken into account when calculating idle time. — idle is recorded only when the ignition is on, — idle is counted regardless of the ignition state After you fill in the parameters on this tab, do not forget to click “Save” to apply your changes.

On this tab you can fill in additional information about the object. Which parameter fields are available is determined by the administrator of your contract. The administrator manages the fields in the account of the admin panel . After the administrator configures the additional fields, you can see and fill them in on this tab. If you later need to display more information about the object, the administrator will add the corresponding fields. This is an example of the tab with additional fields in the user interface: After you fill in the parameters on this tab, do not forget to click “Save” to apply your changes.

On this tab you can specify parameters that help you manage fuel consumption. Summer and winter fuel consumption — specify fuel consumption for winter and summer separately to understand which changes in consumption are caused by seasonal factors and not only by how the vehicle is used. Period start — use the calendar to select the start dates of the summer and winter periods for calculating fuel consumption by season. Fuel consumption per engine hour — this parameter tracks fuel consumption not only by distance traveled but also by engine running time. For example, it is specified for equipment that often works in one place: construction and agricultural machinery or generators. Idle fuel consumption Fuel type: diesel, AI-80, AI-92, AI-95, AI-98, gas Fuel tank capacity — specify the parameter for tracking fuel consumption and level Fuel cost After you fill in the parameters on this tab, do not forget to click “Save” to apply your changes.

On this tab you can attach documents and files to the object so that the necessary information is at hand. Upload files in doc, png, txt, excel, and pdf formats. This tab is available right after the object is created. How to add a file On the tab, click the “Add file” button 2. In the pop-up window, enter a description of the file 3. Upload a file from your computer using the “Choose file” button 4. Click “Save” The uploaded files appear on the tab.

The object menu is a list of actions you can perform with the selected object. To open the object menu, right-click the object in the object list. The set of actions available in the object menu depends on the modules connected to your contract. Let s look at the main actions you can perform with an object through the menu. Current track The current track shows where the object is now and how it has been moving recently. You see its location and route on the map. 1. Current route of the object 2. Movement history player With the player you can review how the object moved: its route, speed, and travel time. 3. Follow the object on the track Turn on the “Follow” function to watch the object's movement online. 4. Playback speed You can increase or decrease the playback speed. To finish viewing the route, click the cross. Follow object Click the “Follow object” function — and you see its location on the map. To cancel following, click the cross. If you click the object icon, an information tooltip about it appears. Map The map is a tool for viewing objects in detail. When you use this function, a mini window with a map opens; you can move it around the screen and resize it as you like. You can view the locations of several objects in turn. Select several objects in the list at the same time — each object is shown in close-up one after another. This way, the location of all selected objects is always available. Open mini maps are saved in the browser and are restored automatically after the page is refreshed Edit To change the object information, select the edit function. The object card opens, where you can make changes. To quickly open the object card for editing, simply double-click the object in the list with the left mouse button. Highlight with color Highlight with color is a quick way to highlight important objects in the list so that you notice them right away. Sensors When you click this item of the object menu, you go to the sensor settings window. Here you can add and configure the object s sensors. Points The “Points” item takes you to a window with information about raw points. Raw points are unprocessed information that sensors collect from the device in real time. What raw points include: The exact time the data was received Location — latitude, longitude, altitude Driving speed Direction Number of satellites Readings of additional sensors, for example temperature, fuel level, battery charge, and pressure sensors View the object s status data in a table or on a chart. 1 — Select the period for building the points report. In this report you can select data for only one day for one object 2 — Build the report 3 — Build a chart. Select sensors, and their values are displayed on the chart To download the raw points data, click . Temporary blocking Temporary blocking is a pause mode for an object in the system. When the equipment is not in use, for example in winter, you can suspend data collection and the deduction of the subscription fee. This function suits, for example, seasonal equipment that operates only part of the year. Clone When you have similar objects with small differences, use cloning. It is a quick way to create a copy of an existing object. The system automatically copies all settings, but in the card you need to enter a new name for the object and change the unique identifier. Import WLN This function transfers objects from the Wialon system to PILOT. To learn how to work with this function, see here. History When you click “History” in the object menu, you go to the “History” section, where you can view all the information about this object s past movements and status. Delete object When you delete an object, all its data and history disappear. If you need to restore the information, contact the system administrator. Menu for working with several objects In the object list, select several objects while holding the Ctrl key on the keyboard 2. Right-click the objects — the menu for working with several objects opens Edit The “Edit” button is activated only when you select objects with the same device type. Select objects with the same device type for bulk editing. When you click “Edit”, a window with settings for the selected objects opens. In this window you can configure parameters for all the selected objects at once. Sensor templates The “Sensor templates” button opens a window with ready-made sensor settings. When you apply a template, the ready-made sensor parameters appear in each object. A sensor template can be applied only to objects with devices of the same type. Export agents The “Export agents” function saves information about the selected objects to a separate file in JSON format. It contains information about the vehicle, the device, and the sensors. Follow object Click the “Follow object” function — and you see their location on the map. History When you click “History”, you go to the “History” section, where you can view all the information about the past movements and status of the selected objects. Move to group This function moves the selected objects to a group. In the “Move to group” window, select a group and click the “Move” button. How to create and work with an object group is described in the next article.

The “Online” tab contains the object list. In the list you can monitor the status of objects and control their parameters. Working with the list Here we look at the functions for working with the list. 1. Add object If you need to add a new object , click this button. Then fill in the information about the new object in the card that opens. After that, the new object appears in the list. 2. Object status filter Filter the objects in the list by status: Blocked objects Parking — objects that have been stationary for longer than the specified time Idle in zone — objects that have been stationary for longer than the specified time in a certain geofence Moving — objects that are moving Speeding — objects that exceed the set speed No connection — objects with which there is currently no connection Here you can also configure the color indication for each status. The color indication of statuses in the list highlights each object in a specific color that shows its state. Just by looking at the list, you immediately understand what is happening with an object — whether it is stationary, moving, or has some special condition. How to configure status colors: 1. In the status filter list, select the “Configure” button. 2. In the window that opens, select your own color for each object status 3. Click the “Save” button — the status colors are updated Use the “Reset to default” button if you need to restore the standard palette settings. To enable color status in the object list, click the special button When you configure status colors, the new colors are also displayed in the statuses on the top panel. With the standard palette, the statuses on the top panel look like this: Let's configure a color palette for the statuses, for example: In the object list it looks like this: The status colors on the top panel match the configured color palette. When you click a status on the top panel, the list automatically shows only the objects with that status. For example, click the “moving” status — and only moving objects remain in the list. 3. Color objects by status This function helps you visually determine the state of an object in the list. When you click the “Color object name in the list” button, you can choose one of two options: 1. Default — object names are displayed without color highlighting 2. By status — object names are highlighted in different colors depending on their status according to the configured color palette. To enable color highlighting of objects, select the “By status” coloring. Each object is colored in a specific color depending on its status. 4. Change the list view type To change the list view type, click . Here you can choose how objects are displayed in the list — by groups, tags, geofences, or simply as a list. 5. Object search filter To quickly find the object you need, just start typing any letter or digit. The system automatically filters the list, showing only the objects whose name or parameters contain the entered value. 6. Object highlighting Enter the name, number, or any other value of the object you are looking for, and that object is highlighted in the list. 7. Export objects to an Excel file Download the object list in Excel format for printing, sending, or storage. 8. Print the object list 9. Add an object group How to create and work with a group of objects is described below. 10. Import from WLP A function that transfers objects from the Wialon system to PILOT. To learn how to work with this function, see here. 11. Refresh the object list When you work with the object list, the data may change in real time, for example objects may change their status. To refresh the object list and see their current status, click this button. Configuring the object list Configure the object list table the way you like. Select which parameter columns to display, and configure their sorting and filters. How to configure the object list table: 1. In the header of any column, click the arrow . A menu with the column settings appears: Sorting data in ascending or descending order Selecting columns to display Filtering data by the selected column 2. To configure which columns to show: Click “Columns” — a list of parameters available for display in the table column opens Select the checkboxes next to the parameters you want to see If you need to add new parameters to display in the columns, contact the administrator. Additional parameter fields are created in the vehicle field editor in the admin panel. Filtering data by the selected column The table columns have filters that help you quickly find the objects you need by specified parameters. Types of column filters: Selection list — select one or more values from the list with checkboxes. For example, to filter objects by type, open the filter in the “Type” column and select the required value from the drop-down list. The table immediately shows only the objects that match the selected type. Search bar — start typing a value, and the table filters the objects by the query. For example, to filter objects by geofences, open the filter in the “Geofences” column and enter a value in the search field. The table shows the objects that match the query. Object groups Objects can be combined into groups by any criteria to organize the list. Groups can also be used to grant access rights to several objects at once. How to create a group: Click the “Add group” button in the workspace In the window that opens, enter the group name 3. Click “Save” If you mark the group as private, it is visible only to the user who created it. How to work with groups To add an object to a group, drag it to the required group. To perform an action with a group: Right-click the group 2. And select an action: Rename Highlight with color in the list Import objects — upload objects as a list Delete To delete a group, first move the objects out of it. To show or hide the list of all objects in the group, click these icons and .

Tooltip in the object list In the object list you can find additional information about an object in a pop-up tooltip. The additional information may include mileage, location, presence in geofences, speed, the object icon, sensor values, and custom fields configured by the user. To view the information in the tooltip, hover over the object in the list. For the tooltip to be displayed in the object list, select the “Show object tree tooltips” option in “Personalization” . Tooltip on the map When you select objects in the list with a checkbox, they are automatically displayed on the map. To open the tooltip, left-click the object icon on the map. How to configure the contents of the tooltip: Go to “Contract settings” Go to the “Personalization” tab Find the “Tooltip elements” and “Additional tooltip elements” sections 4. Select the elements to display in the object tooltip — select the checkbox in the required field 5. Click “Save settings” on the “Personalization” tab

PILOT checks the time in the data transmitted by the tracker. If the data is too old or contains a date from the future, a red error icon appears in the object list next to the object s status. The object may still appear online, but new points may not appear on the map. The “Online” status shows that the tracker maintains a connection with the system. The error icon helps you understand why the incoming data does not update the object s position. How to view the details Click the red icon next to the object. The “Data error” window opens with the following information: Current problem — the tracker transmits data that is too old or data with a date from the future Last correct update — the time of the last update with a correct time Error started — when the system detected the current problem Last incorrect packet — the date and time specified by the tracker in the latest data with the error. This time may differ from the time the system received it. What to do when the error appears 1. Check the date, time, and time zone in the tracker settings. Incorrect settings may cause the error 2. Check time synchronization. If the tracker receives time from GPS or GLONASS, make sure synchronization works. If the time is not updated, restart the tracker 3. If the error persists, contact the specialist who services the hardware. Give them a screenshot of the “Data error” window. The specialist will check the firmware, the data transmission settings, and the reason why old data or data with a date from the future is being sent 4. If you need help from PILOT technical support, specify the object name and the tracker ID, and attach a screenshot of the “Data error” window. The screenshot shows the type of problem and the update times The red icon next to the object disappears automatically after data with a correct time is received. The OK button only closes the window and does not eliminate the error.

A sensor is a device that collects and transmits data about a specific parameter or state of an object. For example, sensors help monitor the fuel level in tanks, engine operation, the temperature of cargo in refrigerated vehicles, air humidity, and other indicators. In this section we cover: — how to add a new sensor and configure its parameters — which sensor types exist in the system — how to use sensor templates — how to work with handlers — how to create sensor groups — how to assign tags — how to copy sensor settings

Before adding a sensor, check that the device sends the specified parameter. If you add a sensor with a parameter that the device does not send, the sensor will not work. To add a sensor: Open the object menu. To do this, right-click the object in the object list 2. Click the “Sensors” tab in the object menu 3. In the window that opens, on the “Sensors” tab, click the button for adding a sensor In the window that appears, select the sensor type by purpose. For example, a battery charge sensor Fill in the required fields for adding a sensor — enter the name and description, and select the field in which the device sends the values the sensor needs. Configure the necessary parameters 6. Click the “Save” button. Check that the sensor appears in the list of active sensors To check that the sensor works correctly and transmits data: 1. Open the object menu 2. Go to the “Points” tab 3. Here you see the values transmitted by all sensors Sensor parameters window When you add or edit a sensor, its parameters window opens. To open the parameters window to edit a sensor, double-click the sensor in the list. The following fields are filled in in the sensor parameters window: Sensor parameter field Description Purpose When adding a sensor, select its purpose from the drop-down list Type Type of the sensor by its operating principle, for example two-position, pulse, or discrete. When you select the sensor purpose, the system determines the sensor type automatically Name This is a required field. Enter the sensor name to distinguish it in the system. For quick filling, use the icon — copy the sensor purpose. If the object has several sensors of the same type, enter a unique name Description This is a required field. Enter the sensor description. For quick filling, use the icon Field This is a required field. From the drop-down list, select the field that shows the value for the sensor Unit of measurement Define the units in which the sensor values are displayed, for example: liters, kilometers Group Select a group for the sensor. To learn how to create a group of sensors, see here Conversion formula Use a formula to calculate the sensor values. A mathematical formula helps recalculate raw data and correct the sensor readings Tags Assign a tag to the sensor. To learn how to create a tag , see here Minimum and maximum value Set the range of valid values. This way, the sensor filters out incorrect readings Minimum and maximum threshold Configure the working range of the sensor — the valid value limits within which the sensor operates normally. If the readings go outside this range, the system records a deviation On and off names Specify the names for the “on” and “off” states In addition to filling in the sensor parameters, you can select additional options with checkboxes. Additional options Description Event filter The event filter protects against accidental sensor triggering caused by brief interference. It sets after how many data packets or seconds the system records a change in the sensor state. It applies to on and off sensors. In the filter you can configure two parameters: the number of received data packets and the time in seconds. For example, if you set the value 3, the system confirms turning the sensor on or off only after receiving three packets with this signal. If you set 10 seconds, the system checks whether the sensor state has changed within this period Create events The sensor records changes, and the system creates entries in the event log Filter values The function discards unreliable sensor readings. The value received from the sensor is converted by the formula and then compared with the valid range specified in the calibration table. If the value is outside the valid range, it is discarded and not taken into account. Show in tooltips The sensor and its values are displayed in the tooltips of the object Fixed values The function sets specific values at which the sensor is considered on or off. It is used when the sensor transmits fixed numbers rather than a range. Specify the known values, for example, if the sensor transmits the value = 38 when on and 37 when off, all other values are ignored. Save history When history is saved, sensor readings are reflected in reports. If history is not saved, only the current readings are available Count engine hours The system tracks the running time of the engine or equipment based on the sensor data Show sensor value in the app If the option is on, the sensor value is visible in the smartphone app. If it is off, the value is not displayed in the mobile version. Aggregation period (Aggregation period) The minimum time interval over which the sensor data is grouped (aggregated) into one event. If off — the system takes into account every individual message from the sensor. Because of this, reports may show many short triggers, false on and off switches, and the sensor's operating intervals look “ragged” and unstable. If on and set to, for example, 120 seconds — the system combines all sensor values received within this interval into one event. That is, the sensor stops “flickering” because of frequent messages and works more stably. Additional settings for some sensors: Number of points for detecting a threshold exceedance In a temperature sensor, this parameter determines how many times in a row the sensor must record a threshold exceedance for the system to treat the event as real. For example, if set to 6, the system reacts only after six consecutive confirmed measurements. This helps avoid false triggers caused by brief interference. Smoothing coefficient The smoothing coefficient helps make the data more accurate. It removes sharp jumps in the readings, which are often erroneous How the smoothing coefficient works: 1. The system takes several measurements before and after each measurement point 2. Removes the highest and lowest values, which may be errors 3. Calculates the average of the remaining measurements 4. Uses this average instead of the original value You can configure the smoothing coefficient — n. It is a number that determines how many points to the left and right of each measurement on the chart are used for smoothing. The higher the coefficient, the stronger the smoothing. For example, if n = 3, the system takes 3 points to the left and 3 to the right of each measurement. The choice of n depends on how detailed the data you need is and how strongly you want to remove fluctuations in the measurements Working temperature range Valid threshold values within which the temperature is considered normal “Active” switch Turns the analysis of refuels and fuel drains by the sensor on or off. For fuel sensors: all enabled sensors of the object are first summed to obtain the total volume of fuel in the vehicle, and only then are events searched for in the sum. If turned off — the sensor is used as a regular one, without automatic event search. Removal of symmetric refuels or drains The function excludes from the report records of refuels or fuel drains with an insignificant change in fuel level. For example, if the sensor recorded a brief change in fuel level caused by a road slope or a technical failure, the system filters out these records

PILOT has two kinds of calibration tables: a calibration table with a chart and a calibration table with text states. You can edit a calibration table only after the new sensor is saved. A calibration table is a lookup reference that converts technical sensor readings into meaningful values. Let s look at an example of using a calibration table for a fuel level sensor. Suppose we have a fuel tank of non-standard shape, so its volume cannot be expressed as a simple function of the fuel level. We install a fuel level sensor in it that works on the rheostat principle. It does not measure the fuel volume directly but changes its electrical resistance depending on the liquid level. As a result, the sensor outputs data in ohms rather than liters. The sensor resistance range is 10 to 180 ohms. To determine the fuel level in the tank correctly, you need to perform calibration and create a correspondence table. Tank calibration: 1. Empty the tank completely and record the minimum sensor resistance value 2. Then pour in fuel in portions, for example 10 liters each, and record the resistance readings 3. Record the sensor readings after each pour 4. Repeat the process until the tank is full 5. Create the calibration table – the correspondence between the fuel level in liters and the sensor resistance in ohms Example of a calibration table for a 100-liter tank Fuel level, l Sensor resistance, ohm 0 180 10 160 20 140 30 120 40 100 50 80 60 60 70 50 80 40 90 20 100 10 When the sensor transmits, for example, 100 ohms, the system uses the calibration table to determine that the tank contains about 40 liters of fuel. If the sensor transmits 110 ohms, the system calculates that the fuel level is about 35 liters. Calibration table with a chart A type of calibration table in which sensor readings are converted to real values using a dependency chart. The X axis shows the sensor readings, and the Y axis shows the real values of the measured quantity. A chart is built between the entered points and determines the real value for a sensor reading. This type of calibration table is often used for fuel level, weight, temperature, and humidity sensors. How to create a table You can configure the table in the sensor parameters window or upload a ready-made one from a file. A configured table can be saved to a file and used for other similar sensors. To open the calibration table, click “Edit”. Edit table How to add values to the table: Click “Add” 2. Enter the real amount of fuel and the value the sensor shows 3. Click “Save” 4. Repeat the steps for all the required readings Example of a filled-in table Calibration table with text states This type of calibration table is used for multi-position sensors and converts the sensor s numeric values into statuses that are easy for the user to understand. Let s look at an example of using this type of table. For example, we have a multi-position GPS antenna sensor that shows the signal level. A GPS receiver measures signal strength in dBm, where values are usually in the range from -160 dBm to -120 dBm. In the table, we convert the technical values sent by the sensor into understandable statuses: “No signal”, “Weak signal”, “Medium signal”, “Good signal”. When the sensor sends a value, for example -135 dBm, the system finds the match in the table and converts it into a text status — “Weak signal”. The text status is shown in the object s tooltip and in reports . Such a calibration table can be used for different parameters, for example, you can set value ranges for temperature measurement: “Cold” — 0–10°C, “Warm” — 10–25°C, “Hot” — 25°C and above; or display the battery charge not as a percentage but as the statuses “Low”, “Medium”, “Full”. How to add a calibration table for multi-position sensors: Open the sensor parameters window In the “Calibration table” section, click “Edit” In the calibration table window, click “Add” Fill in the columns with the minimum and maximum sensor values, Set the text statuses in the “Semantics” column Select an icon and a Background color for the status. The status color is used on charts and in history when building the track. Click “Save”

Added sensors appear in the list on the “Sensors” tab. The list has columns with the same names as the sensor parameters. Configure the sensor list table the way you like. Select which parameter columns to display and configure their sorting. How to configure the sensor list table: 1. In the header of any column, click the arrow . A menu with the column settings appears: Sorting data in ascending or descending order Selecting columns to display 2. To configure which columns to show: Click “Columns” — a list of parameters available for display in the table column opens Select the checkboxes next to the parameters you want to see. How to delete a sensor To delete a sensor, click in the sensor list.

In this article we look at the sensor types that exist in the PILOT system, what they are used for, and which parameters you need to configure for some of them to work correctly. — what sensor types exist and how they work — how to choose the sensor purpose and its type — how to configure a fuel sensor Sensor types The sensor type determines which parameters it controls in the monitoring system. Let s look in more detail at which sensor types exist and what they are used for in PILOT. When adding a sensor, first select its purpose. The type is determined automatically, but you can change it if necessary. 1 — Sensor purpose 2 — Sensor type Sensor types by operating principle Text sensors Displays the device state in words. For example, instead of technical codes, a lock sensor outputs the messages “Lock open” and “Lock closed”. Discrete sensors Pass on data in the form in which the device sent it. To get an exact value, this data can be converted using calibration tables or formulas . For discrete sensors you can enable the alerts function. When the sensor state changes, the system sends notifications by e-mail or SMS. Pulse sensors Count the number of pulses between readings. For example, an engine hours sensor that records the number of pulses to calculate equipment running time. Two-position sensors Record two states of an object: on — off or open — closed. The system determines its state by a range of values: if the reading falls between the set minimum and maximum, the sensor is considered on, otherwise off. Discrete integral sensors Work on the principle of discrete sensors but additionally accumulate the received values. For example, such a sensor can count the total number of events — how many times the engine was started or the body doors were opened during a shift. Pulse integral sensors An analog of pulse sensors, but with the function of accumulating the total number of pulses. For example, such sensors can count the total number of pulses to analyze long-term equipment operation — the total engine running time over a month or the total mileage of a vehicle over a quarter. Two-position inverse sensors Work the same way as two-position sensors but show the state in reverse order. For example, you need the alarm to go off when a door is opened without authorization. A regular sensor may fail to trigger because of the wiring specifics, while an inverse sensor “flips” the signal: when the door is open, the sensor shows “closed”; when it is closed, it shows “open”, to guarantee that the alarm is triggered. This way, the sensor insures the system against errors. Multi-position sensors Used to register readings that can take several values. The values are interpreted based on a calibration table. For example, temperature, humidity, or pressure sensors. Composite sensors Combine data from several sensors. For example, combining data from a fuel sensor and an engine hours sensor to calculate fuel consumption per unit of time. Special sensors Such sensors are designed to collect highly specialized information. For example, an RFID sensor can recognize objects and people, a GPS sensor determines the exact location, a CAN bus sensor collects the vehicle s technical parameters, and a people counter counts the number of visitors in a room. Sensor table Sensor purpose Operating principle Description Ignition sensor Two-position The sensor is used to monitor engine operation and account for vehicle running time. When the engine is running, the sensor shows the value = 1; when it is off, the value = 0 Fuel sensor Discrete Tracks the fuel level in the tank. To learn how to configure a fuel sensor, read below Special equipment operation sensor Two-position Collects data on the start and end of equipment operation. It has two states: on — the sensor shows the value = 1, and off = 0 Battery charge sensor Discrete Tracks the battery state and records charge levels GPS antenna sensor Two-position Determines the presence or absence of a GPS signal. It has two states: on — the sensor shows the value = 1, or off = 0 Temperature sensor Discrete Monitors the temperature of cargo, for example in refrigerated vehicles, or of the environment. You must set the minimum and maximum temperature values at which the sensor triggers SOS button Two-position A sensor whose non-zero value allows marking a message as an alarm. You need to set the minimum and maximum values for the sensor to trigger Engine lock status Two-position Shows the current state of the mechanism: locked or unlocked CAN mileage Discrete Tracks the distance the vehicle has traveled Liquid volume sensor Discrete Monitors the liquid level in a container Passenger flow Composite Determines the number of boarding and exiting passengers and the direction of their movement Fuel consumption Pulse Measures the amount of fuel consumed through pulses. When a certain volume of fuel passes through the sensor, it gives an electrical signal. To measure consumption correctly, configure the “Pulses per liter” parameter, which specifies how many pulses the sensor produces when one liter of fuel passes through iButton Special Used to identify drivers with iButton — a compact electronic key with a built-in chip. On contact with the reader, the key transmits its unique number, which PILOT uses to identify the driver. The iButton purpose can also be used to identify the driver by a Mettax camera Accelerometer Discrete Determines changes in speed and direction of movement. Records acceleration along the X, Y, Z axes and detects collisions. Fuel type Multi-position Used to monitor the consumption of several types of fuel, for example gas or gasoline. How this sensor detects a refuel: 1. Refuel detection The sensor constantly monitors the fuel level and records the readings. The system takes 5 consecutive fuel level measurements Compares the difference between the first and the last measurement If the difference between them is greater than the specified value, the system considers it a refuel. This value is set in the sensor settings. 2. Refuel start When the system has detected a refuel, it analyzes the data for the last 20 minutes. It looks for the measurement point with the lowest fuel level in this time span. The system considers this point the start of the refuel. 3. Refuel end The system understands that the refuel has ended: If five measurements in a row show the same fuel level — the vehicle has been refueled and is standing still If the next measurement shows less fuel than the previous one — the vehicle has been refueled and started moving If the signal disappears for an hour, the system considers that the vehicle's power was cut off, for example the ignition was turned off, which can also mean the end of the refuel A fuel drain is detected the same way as a refuel, except that instead of an increase in the fuel level the system records a sharp decrease. The system detects a refuel or fuel drain by comparing the fuel level at several points. If data arrives too often, increase the number of points in the sensor settings to avoid false triggers. If too rarely, decrease it. Rotation speed Discrete Measures the number of revolutions of the engine or other rotating mechanisms. It is used, for example, to monitor the rotation speed of the engine, a concrete mixer drum, or other equipment. The measurement result is shown in revolutions per minute — RPM Engine hours sensor Discrete Reads the number of pulses between readings to record equipment running time. It is used to account for the running time of the engine or other devices Concrete mixer loading or unloading sensor Two-position Used to track the loading and unloading of materials in construction machinery RFID reader Special Used to read RFID tags and recognize objects or users. An RFID tag is an electronic tag or chip that stores a unique code for identifying an object or a person. It works as a contactless electronic pass Humidity sensor Discrete Used to monitor the humidity level, for example in refrigeration units, warehouses, and other places where it is important to maintain the required humidity. It shows just a number, for example 60%, or an acceptable humidity range, for example, normal is 40-60% Weight sensor Discrete Used to measure the load on a vehicle Lock Text Sends the password to unlock the lock. After it triggers, a new item appears in the object menu — “Open lock” Sleep sensor Two-position Sends a signal that the device is switching to sleep mode. When it is time to go to sleep mode, the device sends a last message with an event number and then stops transmitting data completely Security sensor Two-position Can be in two states: “on” or “off”. For example, such a sensor monitors the opening of a door or window in case of a possible intrusion Battery connection Two-position Determines whether the battery is connected or not Relative odometer Pulse A sensor for calculating mileage from the speedometer or other connected equipment data. It accounts for the distance traveled when GPS/GLONASS data is missing or not accurate enough. The terminal counts pulses between message transmissions, and PILOT sums the received values and converts them into distance. To configure it, specify the number of pulses per kilometer. The value is determined separately for each vehicle because it depends on the installed equipment. For example, if 1000 pulses correspond to one kilometer, enter 1000 in the “Pulses per kilometer” field

The fuel sensor in the system has many parameters. Here we look at how to configure it correctly to get accurate data and record refuel and fuel drain events properly. General sensor settings Purpose — the sensor type in the system Type — the sensor s operating principle, for example “Discrete” Name — the internal name of the sensor shown in the interface Field — the hardware input of the tracker the sensor is connected to Description — additional information about the sensor Units of measurement — usually liters (“l.”) Conversion formula — if you need to correct the data Tags — labels for convenient search and filtering of sensors Detecting refuels and fuel drains To determine refuels and fuel drains correctly, the filtering parameters and trigger thresholds must be configured properly in the system. This helps exclude false events and improve data accuracy. The “Active” switch — turns the analysis of refuels and fuel drains by this sensor on or off. For fuel sensors: all enabled sensors of the object are first summed to obtain the total volume of fuel in the vehicle, and only then are events searched for in the sum. If turned off, the sensor works as a regular one, without searching for refuels and fuel drains. Drain through the return line The “Drain through the return line” function helps detect hidden theft through the return line — the fuel line through which unused fuel returns to the tank. After the function is enabled, the system analyzes abnormal fuel consumption while driving, calculates the volume of a possible drain, and marks the place of the event on the map. Trigger thresholds Refuel threshold — the minimum increase in fuel level that the system considers a refuel Fuel drain threshold — the minimum decrease in fuel level that is recorded as a fuel drain These parameters help to: — ignore minor fluctuations in fuel level — exclude sensor noise — record only real events Driving speed filter The speed filter is used to exclude false events while driving. For example: — fuel consumption on the road is not detected as a fuel drain — fluctuations in fuel level are not counted as a refuel The system analyzes the object s speed at the time of the event and, depending on the selected mode, can ignore points with high speed. Maximum speed for detection (event search) — the speed in km/h below which the vehicle is considered stationary Speed mode — how exactly to check the speed within an event Speed accounting mode options: All points — all points of the event must be below the set speed threshold Start — it is enough for only the first point of the event to be below the speed threshold Any point — the event is counted if at least one point meets the condition (for example, is in parking) Average speed — the system compares the average speed of the event with the set threshold Off — disables the speed check. In this mode, refuels and fuel drains are recorded regardless of speed Coefficient — checks whether enough points have a speed below the threshold. It fine-tunes the filtering with additional parameters: — Minimum share of slow points — defines the percentage of event points that must be at low speed. For example: a value of 0.5 means at least 50% — Minimum parking duration — sets the total time during which the object must be at low speed This mode handles situations where the beginning of a refuel or its “tail” falls on a short stretch of movement, but the vehicle was actually stationary most of the time Fuel change rate filter These parameters let you distinguish real events from natural fuel consumption. Minimum refuel rate — the minimum rate of fuel level increase (l/h) for an event to be considered a refuel. If the fuel level rises too slowly, the event is not considered a refuel. Minimum fuel drain rate — the minimum level drop (l/h) for an event to be considered a fuel drain. If the fuel decreases more slowly than the set value, the event is ignored. Sensitivity to sensor noise Smoothing coefficient — the degree of chart smoothing before analysis. It is used when there is noise in the fuel sensor data. The higher the value, the smoother the chart and the fewer sharp jumps, which are often caused by sensor errors. Removal of symmetric events This function helps exclude from the report false operations in which a refuel and a fuel drain occur with almost identical volumes (for example, a road slope or a technical failure). The “Remove symmetric refuels/drains” switch — enables the search for “drain → refuel” or “refuel → drain” pairs with very close volumes Maximum difference, % — the allowed difference in the pair s volumes in percent Maximum difference, l — how much the volumes in liters may differ. Maximum distance (interval between events), h — the time span within which events are considered a “pair”, for example 12 hours. Watch the YouTube video that shows how to set up the refuel and fuel drain detector . https://youtu.be/9YfvN5r7zGA

The “Relative odometer” sensor calculates the object s mileage from the number of pulses transmitted by the terminal. It suits hardware that counts pulses before sending a data packet and starts a new count after sending. PILOT adds up the values from the received messages and converts them to kilometers. The “Pulses per kilometer” coefficient is used for the calculation. Configure the sensor separately for each object: the number of pulses per kilometer depends on the vehicle and the installed hardware. Before setting up, make sure that: — the terminal transmits the number of pulses in a separate field — each value contains the number of pulses counted since the previous packet was sent — the number of pulses corresponding to one kilometer of travel is known If the terminal transmits a constantly increasing total counter, the “Relative odometer” sensor with the “Pulse” type is not suitable for such data. How to add the sensor Add a new sensor to the object 3. In the “Purpose” field, select “Relative odometer”. 4. Make sure the “Type” field is set to “Pulse” 5. In the “Name” field, enter a descriptive name for the sensor, for example “Relative odometer” 6. In the “Field” field, specify the parameter in which the terminal transmits the number of pulses 7. If necessary, fill in the “Conversion formula”. If the terminal transmits a ready number of pulses and no additional conversion is required, leave the field empty 8. In the “Pulses per kilometer” field, enter the number of pulses corresponding to one kilometer of travel 9. If necessary, turn on “Filter values” to exclude incorrect readings 10. Click “Save” After saving, PILOT starts adding up the values from the selected field and calculating mileage using the specified number of pulses per kilometer. Calculating mileage from pulses A pulse is a signal the terminal receives from connected equipment while the vehicle is moving. The greater the distance the vehicle covers, the more pulses the terminal records. In each packet, the terminal transmits the number of pulses accumulated since the previous packet was sent. PILOT adds up these values for the selected period and calculates mileage with the formula: Mileage, km = sum of pulses ÷ number of pulses per kilometer For example, the sensor settings specify 1000 pulses per kilometer. During a trip, the terminal transmitted three values: 200, 350, and 450. First, PILOT adds up the pulses: 200 + 350 + 450 = 1000 pulses Then it calculates the mileage: 1000 ÷ 1000 = 1 km The value in the “Pulses per kilometer” field must be greater than zero. The more accurately the coefficient is specified, the more accurately the mileage is calculated. How to determine the number of pulses per kilometer If the coefficient is unknown, determine it with a test trip: 1. Record the initial mileage and pulse counter readings 2. Drive a test distance. For a more accurate result, it is better to choose a long enough section, for example 10 kilometers 3. Determine the total number of pulses received during the trip 4. Divide the number of pulses by the distance traveled: Pulses per kilometer = number of pulses ÷ distance, km For example, over 10 kilometers the terminal transmitted 12,500 pulses: 12,500 ÷ 10 = 1250 pulses per kilometer Enter 1250 in the “Pulses per kilometer” field. After calibration, make another test trip and compare the calculated mileage with the actual one. If the values differ, refine the coefficient. Checking the calculation Compare the calculated mileage with the vehicle s actual mileage on the test section. If the values differ: — check whether the field with the number of pulses is selected correctly — make sure the terminal starts a new count after sending each packet — adjust the “Pulses per kilometer” value — check the completeness of the received data If some packets did not reach PILOT, the calculated mileage may be lower than the actual one.

Templates are a ready-made set of parameters used to quickly configure devices of the same type. A sensor template can be applied only to objects with devices of the same type. For example, a template from Teltonika FMB120 suits only Teltonika FMB120 There are two types of templates: Local templates — your own settings that you create yourself on an object Global templates — ready-made settings that any user can use How to create a local template: Configure the sensors the way you need 2. On the “Sensors” tab, click the “Save template” button 3. Enter the template name and description 4. Click “Save as new” How to apply a template to one object: Go to the object you want to apply the template to Sensor templates suit only objects with the same type of GPS device. If you created a template for one object, it works only on other objects with the same device. Open the sensors window through the object menu On the “Sensors” tab, select the saved template from the drop-down list of templates 1 — Apply template 2 — Delete template 4. Click the “Apply template” button 5. If necessary, delete the old sensors 6. Click “Apply” — the sensors from the template appear on the “Sensors” tab To remove a template from the list, click the cross. How to apply a template to several objects: In the object list, select several objects while holding the Ctrl key on the keyboard 2. Right-click the objects — the menu for working with several objects opens 3. In the menu, select “Sensor templates” 4. In the window that opens, select the saved template 5. Click “Apply template” Where to find global templates: On the “Sensors” tab in the drop-down list of templates 2. In the “Sensor templates” window when working with several objects

A conversion formula is a mathematical expression applied to the data received from a sensor. Why apply a formula: To correct sensor readings, for example, a formula lets you fix inaccuracies in sensor readings To bring raw sensor data to real physical quantities. For example, a sensor outputs numbers from 0 to 1000, and the formula converts them into the real liters of fuel in the tank To convert units of measurement, for example, kilometers to miles or liters to gallons To combine data, for example, a formula can use values from different sensors to produce new indicators In the sensor settings window, the formula is entered in a special field The formula is applied to the data immediately after it is received from the sensor, before the calibration table is used. The formula must start with one of the following characters: • arithmetic signs: +, -, *, / • the equals sign: = In a formula you can use: • mathematical operations: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/) • parentheses ( ) to specify the order of operations Simple formulas Used for simple operations such as multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction. The original sensor value is substituted into the formula automatically. Let s look at an example of applying a formula. Suppose we have a battery charge sensor that transmits the value in millivolts. In the raw points, we find the sensor value: Vsource = 9246. To display the familiar sensor value in volts, the raw value must be divided by 1000. In the sensor settings window, in the “Formula” field, we write the formula: /1000. The final sensor value is calculated by the formula Vbattery/1000: The system takes the current sensor value in the raw points 2. Divides this value by 1000 3. The result becomes the new sensor value The final value of the battery sensor in volts is shown in the object tooltip — 9.25 V. Examples of simple formulas Formula Result *10 Multiply the original value by 10 /1000 Divide the original value by 1000 /25.5+7 Divide the value by 25.5 and add 7 to it /100+(7*3-2)*4 A more complex example using parentheses In formulas, decimal fractions are written with a period, not a comma. For example: 25.4, 1.75 Variables in a formula Data from sensor fields and standard variables can be substituted into a formula. All values to be substituted into the formula are enclosed in %% characters Standard variables used in a formula: %S% — speed %A% — altitude %D% — direction %P% or %satsinview% — number of satellites %ts% — time of the current packet %ts1% — time of the previous packet Time is used in Unix timestamp format — the number of seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970. %value% — value of the current sensor All other values are taken directly from the names in the raw points data packet sent by the sensor. For example: %Vbattarey% — battery charge sensor value %GSM% — mobile signal level value %HDOP% — horizontal dilution of precision Enclose the required parameter name in %%, and during the formula calculation it is replaced with the corresponding value from the data packet. Examples of formulas with variable substitution Formula Result *%GSM% Multiply the original value by the data from the GSM field /%HDOP% Divide the original value by the data from the HDOP field %ts1%-%ts% Get the time difference between the current and the previous packet %ts%/86400 Convert time from seconds to days Complex formulas Complex formulas always start with the = sign. In such formulas the original sensor value is not used automatically. If you need to use the original value, specify it through %value%. These formulas let you perform more complex operations, including using variables, parentheses, and mathematical functions. Examples of complex formulas Formula Result =%value%*2+10 Multiply the current sensor value by 5 and add 10 =%S%*3.6+%value% Convert speed to km/h and add the original value = (%DIN1%+%DIN2%)/%value% Divide the sum of the digital inputs by the original value =7/%value% Divide the number 7 by the original sensor value Conditional operators Conditional operators are a way to set selection logic in a formula. They let a formula take different values depending on whether a certain condition is met. It is similar to a query: “If the condition is true, do one thing, otherwise do another”. A conditional operator is written like this condition ? value_if_yes : value_if_no This expression can be explained as follows: — condition — the expression that is checked, for example, the temperature is above 30 —value_if_yes — the value returned if the condition is true — value_if_no — the value returned if the condition is false Comparison operators The following operators can be used in conditions: Operator Meaning Description == equal to checks for exact equality != not equal to checks for inequality greater than checks whether the left value is greater than the right one less than checks whether the left value is less than the right one = greater than or equal to checks whether the left value is greater than or equal to the right one = less than or equal to checks whether the left value is less than or equal to the right one and checks that all conditions are true || or checks that at least one condition is true Example 1 Suppose we have a digital input sensor field DIN1, and we want to set a condition: If DIN1 equals 1, the result is 22 If DIN1 does not equal 1, the result is 33 The formula looks like this: =(%DIN1% == 1) ? 22 : 33 The system checks the condition: %DIN1% == 1 (whether the DIN1 value equals 1). If the condition is true, 22 is returned. If the condition is false, 33 is returned. Example 2 Suppose we have a temperature sensor field temp, and we want to set a condition: If the temperature is above 30, the result is: temperature * 10. If the temperature is less than or equal to 30, the result is: temperature * 20. The formula looks like this: =(%temp% 30) ? %temp% * 10 : %temp% * 20. The system checks the condition: %temp% 30 (whether the temperature is above 30). If the condition is true, temperature * 10 is returned. If the condition is false, temperature * 20 is returned. Example 3 Suppose we have a temperature sensor with the field temp and a humidity sensor humidity, and we want to set the following condition: If the temperature is above 25 AND the humidity is below 60%, the result is 100 Otherwise, the result is 50 The formula looks like this: =(%temp% 25 %humidity% 60) ? 100 : 50 %temp% 25 is the first condition (the temperature is above 25), %humidity% 60 is the second condition (the humidity is below 60%). The operator means that both conditions must be met. The system checks the conditions and, if both conditions are true, returns 100; if at least one condition is false, it returns 50. PHP functions PHP functions are ready-made tools of the PHP programming language for processing, converting, and formatting data. With PHP functions , apply complex transformations by simply specifying the function name and the value in the formula. All you need to do: 1. Write the function name in the formula 2. Specify in parentheses the value you want to convert 3. And the system automatically takes your data, processes it the required way, and shows the result For example, if you write round (45.78) in a formula, you get the rounded number 46. Functions Description Example substr Extracts part of a string =substr('%Data%', x, y) — returns “y” characters from the Data value starting at position “x” =substr('%FIELD%', 1, 2) — returns 2 characters from the FIELD value starting at position 1 round Rounds a number =round(%AIN1%/1000) — divides the AIN1 value by 1000 and rounds the result hexdec Converts a hexadecimal number to decimal =hexdec('%Param%'), if Param=0A, the function returns 10 dechex Converts a decimal number to hexadecimal = dechex('%Param%'), if Param=255, the function converts 255 to 'FF' decbin Converts a decimal number to binary =decbin('%Param%'), if Param=10, the function returns 1010 hex2bin Converts a hexadecimal notation to binary data =hex2bin ('%Param%'), if Param=4142, the function returns the binary representation 'AB' strrev Reverses a string =strrev('%value%'), if value=0123d848010000e5, the function converts the value to 5е000010848d3210 bytesrev Reverses hexadecimal bytes =bytesrev('%value%'), value=0123d848010000e5, the function converts the value to e500000148d82301 explode Splits a string into parts by the specified delimiter and returns an array of strings =explode(',','%value%')[2] Suppose the sensor transmits a string of comma-separated values: 90.5,3450,112,43,215 In this case the formula =explode(',','%value%')[2] takes the current sensor reading and splits it into an array: '90.5', '3450', '112', '43', '215', and then extracts the element with index 2 — '112' An array of strings is a list of separate strings numbered from zero. ',' is the delimiter, in this case a comma. The string is split at this character. '%value%' is the string to split. [2] — square brackets are used to access an array element. [2] means “give me the third element”, numbering starts at 0. max Compares several values and returns the largest =max('%value%', 90), if value=85, the function returns 90 min Returns the smallest value =min('%value%', 90), if value=85, the function returns 85 abs Returns the absolute value of a number =abs('%value%'), if value = -15, the function returns 15 str_replace Replaces some characters or words with others str_replace(search, replace, subject) search — what to look for replace — what to replace it with subject — where to look (the string) For example, we need to replace commas with periods in numbers =str_replace(",", ".",'%value%'), if value = 1,234,567, the function outputs — 1.234.567 sqrt Calculates the square root =sqrt('%value%'), if value = 25 , the function returns 5 pow Raises a number to a power =pow('%value%', 3), if value =2, the function returns 8 (that is, 2³) sin Calculates the sine of an angle (in radians) =sin('%value%'), if value= 1.57, the final value is ≈ 1 cos Calculates the cosine of an angle (in radians) =cos('%value%'), if value = 0, the final value is 1 asin Calculates the arcsine (in radians) =asin('%value%'), if value=1, the function returns 1.57 acos Calculates the arccosine (in radians) =acos('%value%'), if value= 0, the function returns 1.57 number_format Formats a number with separators =number_format(1234.56, 2, ',', ' ') the function returns 1 234,56 time Returns the current time in UNIX format — in seconds since January 1, 1970 =time('2023-12-20 12:00:00') array_sum Adds up all numbers in an array =array_sum([1,2,3,4]) — the function returns 10 pack Packs data into a binary format =pack('H*', '4142') — packs 'AB' into binary data unpack Unpacks binary data =unpack('H*', 'AB')[1] — returns '4142' Examples of complex conversions Description Example Converting an unsigned number to a signed number =((%BLE_T1% 3000)?((%BLE_T1%-65535)/100):(%BLE_T1%/100)) If the number is greater than 3000 — subtract 65535 from it and divide by 100 If it is less than or equal to 3000 — divide by 100 This formula is often used for temperature sensors, where negative values are encoded as large positive numbers. Converting a byte sequence (little endian to big endian) =strtoupper(substr(unpack('H*',strrev(hex2bin(%value%)))[1],2,12)) — 1500000124286b01 → 6B2824010000 hex2bin(%value%) — converts a hex string to binary data strrev(...) — reverses the bytes unpack('H*', ...) — converts back to hex substr(..., 2, 12) — takes the required part of the string strtoupper(...) — converts to upper case Division by zero When a formula contains division, be careful with the divisor — the number you divide by. If the divisor is zero, an error occurs, because division by zero is mathematically impossible. For example, the formula =1000/%DIN1% causes an error if the DIN1 sensor value is 0 or undefined. In this case, use a conditional operator to check the divisor: =(%DIN1%==0) ? 0 : 1000/%DIN1%. The system checks the condition: %DIN1% == 0 (whether the DIN1 value equals zero). If the condition is true, the result is 0. If the condition is false, 1000 is divided by the DIN1 value. How to check that a formula works When you apply a formula, make sure it converts the data correctly. Check the formula using the “Test” button: Click the “Test” button in the “Formula” field. The system shows values you can use to check the formula specified in the handler. You can select ready-made values or enter your own. 3. After that, click the “Test” button again, and the system shows the result of applying the formula: correct or incorrect. Where else formulas are used Formulas in PILOT can be used not only for processing sensor data. You can use formulas in the “Object card” or when working with the “Notifications” module. The principle of how they work is the same everywhere — the same writing rules and the same mathematical operations.

Handlers are tools that help convert and process raw sensor data into understandable values. Instead of writing complex formulas for every sensor each time, you can create one handler and use it wherever you need it. Suppose you have a vehicle on-board network voltage sensor that transmits values in millivolts. In the raw points, we find the sensor value: Vsource = 14592 To see the familiar sensor reading in volts, the value must be divided by 1000. We can create a handler that we will then use in other sensors where the sensor value needs to be divided by 1000. How to create a handler In the sensors window, find the “Handlers” tab On the tab, click “Add” 3. Enter a name for the handler. This name will be used later in the “Formula” field in the sensor settings window. The field must contain only Latin letters, digits, and signs 4. In the “Formula” field, write the formula that this handler will use. If the formula refers to the sensor data field that the sensor transmits, use the %% characters around the field name, for example, %fuel_1% or %value% 5. Add a description of the handler so you know what it is used for 6. Click “Save” How to set up a calibration table In a handler you can set up a calibration table that the handler takes into account. This table helps convert technical sensor readings into understandable values. To set up a calibration table: Click the icon In the calibration table window for the handler, click “Add” 3. Enter the real value and the value the sensor shows 4. Click “Save” 5. Repeat the steps for all the required readings 6. Click “Save” in the calibration table window In the calibration table, select the “Nearest value selection” and “Calibration priority” functions with checkboxes. The “Nearest value selection” function is a method of rounding to the nearest calibration point. When the device receives a value that does not exactly match the recorded points, it needs to calculate the result. If the “Nearest value selection” option is on, the device takes the value from the nearest point of the calibration table. If it is off, it calculates an intermediate value taking the neighboring points into account. The “Calibration priority” function determines the order of data processing when calibrating the sensor. Priority is given to calibration data over measurement data, that is, the system always starts by checking the calibration table, using it as the primary reference. The system first checks whether the value is in the calibration table. If an exact value is found, it uses it. Only if there is no exact match does it apply the standard calculation algorithm. — use these buttons to load a ready-made calibration table from a file or save it to your computer. To delete a value in the table, click . How to apply a handler 1. Open the sensor where you need to apply the handler 2. In the “Formula” field, write the handler name. First enter the “=” sign, then the name of the handler itself, and in parentheses and %% characters the field transmitted by the sensor. For example, =divide(%fuel_1%) 3. Check the handler using the “ Test ” button 4. Click “Save” in the sensor settings window for the handler to be applied to this sensor Examples of using handlers Example 1. How to convert sensor data with a handler Let s create a handler: Enter a name for the handler — divide 2. In the “Formula” field, enter %value%/1000. value is the value sent by the sensor that needs to be divided by 1000. Add a description of the handler — “Division by 1000” Save the handler Let s apply the handler: Go to the settings window of the sensor where the handler needs to be applied. 2. In the “Formula” field, enter the “=” sign and the handler name, and in parentheses and %% characters the value of the on-board network sensor field: =divide(%Vsource%) 3. Check the handler using the “Test” button 4. Click “Save” in the sensor settings window Let s check how the sensor readings are displayed after the handler is applied In the raw points, the on-board network sensor value is: Vsource = 12626 After processing with the formula, the object tooltip shows the real sensor value — 12.6 V. In this example we showed how to perform a simple operation with a handler. But you can also use more complex formulas for it if necessary. Once you create a handler, you can apply it to many sensors of the same type without worrying about possible errors in the formulas. Example 2. How to get the sum and the average of two fuel level sensors Suppose we have two fuel level sensors. And we need to see their total level and the average fuel level. Both sensors must output values in the same units, and each sensor must have its own calibration table configured. Create handlers for each sensor: Handler for sensor 1 Enter a name for the handler — fuel_nav_1 2. In the “Formula” field, enter %t_53lls1% — copy the field name from the card of fuel sensor 1 Save the handler Handler for sensor 2 Name for the handler — fuel_nav_2 2. In the “Formula” field, enter %lls2% — copy the field name from the card of fuel sensor 2 Save the handler Next, create the total fuel sensor: Enter the sensor name and description — Total fuel sensor 2. Select the sensor type — Discrete 3. In the field, specify the stream of one of the existing sensors (for example, t_53lls1) — points will arrive through it and the formula will be recalculated 4. In the formula, enter =fuel_nav_1()+fuel_nav_2() 5. Save the card of the total fuel sensor After that, the total fuel level across the two tanks appears in the raw points and in the object tooltip (if you enabled the display). Let s create one more sensor for the average fuel level: Enter the sensor name and description — Average fuel sensor 2. Select the sensor type — Discrete 4. In the field, specify the stream of one of the sensors (for example, t_53lls1) 5. In the formula, enter =(fuel_nav_1()+fuel_nav_2())/2 6. Save the card of the average fuel sensor In the raw points, check the values of the created sensors. As a result, the object has four sensors: “Fuel sensor 1”, “Fuel sensor 2”, “Total fuel sensor”, and “Average fuel sensor”. The same logic can be used to process data from temperature sensors.

Sensor groups are a way to organize sensors the way that suits you. You can create groups by any criteria that matter for your work. For example: — by measurement type: temperature, pressure, speed — by location: sensors in the cabin, in the engine, on the outer part of the object How to add a sensor group: Click the “Add group” button 2. In the window that opens, enter a name for the new group 3. If necessary, add a description of the group 4. Click “Save” To assign a group to a sensor, open the sensor edit window and select the name in the “Group” field. In the sensor list, sensor groups are displayed in a separate column.

Tags are a tool for grouping sensors by certain parameters. To use tags in the system, go to “Personalization” and enable the “Show global tags” and “Show tag labels” options. How to create a tag for sensors: 1. Click “Add tag” 2. Enter the tag name 3. Select the sensor type from the drop-down list 4. If you wish, add a description. 5. Select an icon and a color for the tag. Selecting a color is required. 6. Click “Save” To assign a tag to a sensor, open the sensor edit window and select the name in the “Tags” field. You can use tags when creating reports , configuring notifications , and defining events .

If you have several similar monitoring objects, you can copy sensor settings from one object to another. 1. Export sensors Copying sensor settings from the current object Open the sensors window of the object you want to copy settings from Click the “Export” button 3. Select with checkboxes which sensor settings you want to copy 4. Click “Export” — the file with the settings is saved to your computer 2. Import sensors Transferring sensor settings to a new object Before importing sensors, make sure you are working with the right object. To do this, check the object's AgentID in the sensors window. 3. AgentID The unique identification number of the object. Open the sensors window for the object you want to copy the settings to 2. Click the “Import” button 3. Find and select the previously saved settings file If necessary, configure the import parameters — click the text “Select import parameters”. A window with settings opens 4. Click “Import”

History is information about an object s past movements and states, including its routes, stops, and sensor readings for a certain period of time. With “History” you can see where an object was, analyze its route and driving speed, as well as sensor data. In this section you will learn: — how to view the movement history of objects — how to work with the track list — how to use the history player — how to display a track on the map — how to view an object s actions — how to work with speed and sensor reading charts

The “History” section helps you track the movements of vehicles and other monitoring objects. Here you can view routes, analyze events, track sensor readings, and get detailed information about trips for a selected period. How to view an object s movement history: 1. Go to the “History” section on the top navigation panel The “Last report” button opens the most recently built history. Select an object from the list by checking its checkbox Specify the time period in one of the following ways: 1 — Use the calendar to select specific dates 2 — Use the quick buttons: “Yesterday”, “Today”, “Week” 3 — Select working days only, if necessary 4 — Add parking information to the history 4. Click the “Search” button 5. In the search results, select with checkboxes the track records of the object that you want to view A track is a line on the map that shows the path of an object s movement. A track consists of points marking the places where the object was at different times. After you select the tracks you are interested in, the following elements are displayed on the screen: 1 — List of selected tracks 2 — Player — a tool for playing back and controlling the viewing of tracks 3 — Events — significant events or changes related to the object 4 — Route on the map 5 — Chart showing the speed or sensor readings of the object during the selected period

In this article we look at the history functions that help you track an object s movement and parameters and work with the obtained data. Track list After you select the time period and the parameters for building the history, the list of tracks is displayed in the search results. A track is a line on the map that shows the path of an object s movement. A track consists of points marking the places where the object was at different times. The list consists of track records with the following parameters: track date, start, stop, duration, distance, and the object s maximum speed. To configure the parameters that affect how a track is built, go to “Object settings” Configure the track list the way you like. Select which parameter columns to display, for example, the duration of parking or stops. How to configure the list of track records: 1. In the header of any column, click the arrow . A menu with the column settings appears, where you can: • Sort the data in ascending or descending order • Select which columns to show on the screen • Group the records by the selected parameter 2. To configure which columns to show: Click “Columns” — a list of parameters available for display in the list opens Select the checkboxes next to the parameters you want to see Buttons below the track list “Follow” — tracks the object on the map in real time “Return to ‘Online’” — returns to the “Online” tab but keeps the player and the track on the map “Close” — removes the records of the selected tracks from the list Player Use the player to view how the object moved in the past. Click the “Start” button to start viewing. Watch the object s movement on the map and on the speed chart at the bottom of the screen. Next to the player you see the date, time, and current speed of the object at a given moment. To speed up viewing, click the speed-up button — it helps you review long routes faster. Track on the map When you select a record in the track list, the system displays the object s route on the map. You can add several tracks to the map at once, for example, to compare the routes of one or several objects over different periods. Tracks can be displayed in different colors depending on the selected parameters. Track color by speed The speed color is configured in the “Speed in color” section on the “Map and geocoding” tab. Sections of the route are colored depending on the driving speed. Track color by sensor readings The track is colored according to the readings of the selected multi-position sensor along the entire route. To display a track with color indication of sensor readings: 1. Make sure the sensor is configured and has colors set in the calibration table 2. Build the object s movement history by selecting tracks in “History” 3. After the track is displayed, find the panel with the list of sensors at the bottom of the map 4. Select the required sensor from the list 5. Click the palette button that appears 6. The track on the map is colored according to the sensor readings at each point of the route To enlarge the map area, collapse the bottom panel with the chart by clicking the button Event markers Important events that occurred during movement, such as fuel drains, speeding, and parking, are marked on the map with special icons. For detailed information about an event, simply click the corresponding marker on the map. Events Events in “History” are actions that occurred with the object. They are displayed on the “Events” tab. On the “Map and geocoding” tab you can configure which types of events are displayed in “History”. To view events in “History”: 1. Build the object s history and select tracks 2. Go to the “Events” tab. All the object s actions on the selected track are displayed here 3. Select the checkboxes next to all the events in the list that you want to see on the map 4. Go to the map to view the selected events on the track Chart The chart shows the driving speed and sensor readings. When you select a track, only the speed is displayed on the chart automatically. To add sensor readings, select the required sensors in the sensor panel. Their values then appear on the chart. To temporarily hide the data of a sensor, click its name to the left of the chart. The name becomes crossed out, and the line with this parameter disappears from the chart. Clicking again restores the display. Click the “Select all sensors” button to display all available readings. To clear the chart of all selected readings, click the “Clear” button .

A report is information collected about monitored objects for a selected period of time. Reports help you track vehicle operation, monitor task completion, find deviations, and make decisions. In this section you will learn: — how to configure access to reports — how to build a report — how to configure report parameters — how to download or print a finished report — which report types are available and what they are for

To set up access to the reports you need, complete three main steps: Select the available reports in the admin panel 2. Assign report rights to specific users 3. Configure how reports are displayed in the general list Setting up reports through the admin panel If you have administrator access: 1. Sign in to the admin panel 2. Go to the “Contracts” tab 3. Select a contract 4. Right-click the selected contract — the context menu opens 5. In the context menu, select “Report list” 6. In the list that appears, select with checkboxes the reports that you want to make available to the contract s users If necessary, change the report name. To do this, click the field in the “Alternative name” column and enter a more familiar name. Setting up reports in the user account Now it is important to specify which reports are available to specific users: 1. In the contract configuration, go to the “Staff and groups” tab 2. Select a user in the list and click the icon 3. A window with the list of reports opens 4. Select with checkboxes the reports you are assigning access to for this user You can either grant access to all reports or limit the list to only the ones needed. Displaying reports in the list To configure which report types are available when creating a new report: In the contract configuration, go to the “Report list” tab Select the report types — select the checkbox next to the required report name 3. Click the “Save settings” button After you configure report display and access rights, you will be able to: View reports in the list Select the report you need to view Work only with the reports you have access to

To build a report: In the main menu, go to the “Reports” section and select an object by checking it in the object list 2. Select the time interval for the report by clicking the calendar icon 3. Select the report type Specify the report parameters: 4. Report breakdown by days, weeks, or no breakdown into intervals 5. Report grouping by dates, to analyze changes in indicators over time, or by monitoring objects, to compare indicators between different objects 6. Sensor groups the report is generated for 7. Click the “Build report” button

After the report is built, you see the results online right away. 1 — Map in the report 2 — Area divider Interactive map Some reports contain an interactive map that helps you see the report data visually. To enlarge the map area, click the screen divider. For example, the map is useful in reports on object movement.
