Find the “Points of interest” (PoI) module and select the check boxes for the permissions you need: Add own POI: create your own points of interest, available only to this user Read non-own POI: view points created by other users Edit non-own POI: edit points created by other users Delete non-own POI: delete points created by other users Each user can create private POIs and at the same time work with shared points according to the assigned rights, which keeps work with the map organized. How to add a point: 1. Click the “Add point” button 2. In the window that opens, fill in the information: — enter the point name — write a description — select a suitable icon and color — specify the group the point will belong to — set the latitude and longitude, or click on the map to specify the point’s location 3. Click “Save” How to edit a point: 1. Double-click the point’s entry in the list 2. In the window that opens, edit the information you need 3. Click “Save” Saving and loading data • To save all points to an Excel file, click the download button • To load points from an Excel file, click the upload button • To refresh the list of points, click the refresh button Working with the map Select points in the list, and they are displayed on the map with the icons you chose. Click a point to see its description. Use the map tools to work with points. For example, measure distances between them or calculate road distances to plan routes.

The “Sales representative” module, also known as “Counterparties”, is used to record and analyze sales representatives’ visits to counterparties. Counterparties are clients, companies, or retail outlets that your company works with. In this article you will learn: — How to upload a list of counterparties — How to work with the list of counterparties — How to add a sales representative — What a universal sales representative is — How to view a sales representative’s counterparties — How to recalculate visit statistics How to upload a list of counterparties The list of counterparties is uploaded to the system from a file. This is usually done by the technical support service at the client’s request. The upload uses the page: https:// server_address /ax/mod_tp_upload_utf8.php where server_address is the address of your server Open the upload page Enter the login and password of the account into which you need to upload counterparties. 2. Prepare the file The file must be in CSV format. It specifies: — the counterparty identifier — the link to the sales representative or vehicle (if used) — the counterparty group — the address of the point (required) — coordinates Upload the file Click “Choose file” Select the prepared CSV file Click “Submit” The system uploads the data, and the counterparties appear in the “Main” section on the “Counterparties” tab. How to work with the list of counterparties On the “Counterparties” tab you can view the list of clients, search for the points you need, and display them on the map. Tools for working with the list are available at the top of the window: Search: helps you find a counterparty by name or address. Start typing a name and the list is filtered automatically. Additional actions are in the upper-right part of the list: Export: exports the current list of counterparties to a file Clear map: removes counterparty markers from the map Show on map: displays counterparties on the map Refresh: refreshes the list and loads current data How to add a sales representative If you need to add a sales representative to the system: 1. Go to the “Main” section. Open the “Online” tab Click “Add object” Fill in the main parameters in the object card Specify the required data: 1 — Vehicle number 2 — Device ID 3 — Device type Specify the group Select the group the object will belong to. If there is no such group, create it in advance. This group usually contains the sales representatives’ objects. In the object card, enter the sales representative’s ID. Universal sales representative By default, reports include only the counterparties assigned to the sales representative. If a sales representative can visit any points, not only the assigned ones, you need to enable the “Universal SR” option In this case, reports will include visits to all counterparties, regardless of assignment. Save the object After saving, the sales representative appears in the list. How to view a sales representative’s counterparties To see the list of counterparties of a specific sales representative: 1. Right-click the sales representative you need to open the context menu 2. Select “Counterparties” The window that opens shows a list of all points assigned to the counterparty. In the window, select the counterparty you need; it is displayed on the map. If you need to clear the map, click the “Clear map” button . The “Recalculate for” button updates counterparty visit statistics for the selected period. If the data has changed or you need to recalculate routes and visits, use this button. How to run a recalculation 1. Enter the number of days for which to update the data (for example, 2 or 7 days). 2. Click the ▶ button 3. The system analyzes the sales representative’s trips for the specified period and updates the information about counterparty visits and routes When finished, a window with brief statistics appears: From date: the period for which the recalculation was run Total: how many counterparties were counted Visits: how many visits were recorded Execution time: how long the calculation took Click OK to close the window.

The “Control room” module is designed for monitoring and managing object parameters in the system. It helps you track events related to objects and simplifies working with notifications and event-handling algorithms. With this module you can not only receive notifications about events but also configure exactly what the system should do when such an event occurs. The module was previously called GARM. This name may still appear in some places in the interface. The new name, “Control room”, is now in use and will eventually replace the old one completely. Main functions of the module: Event monitoring The system tracks events related to objects and notifies you about them, for example, when parameters deviate or a state changes. Event-handling algorithms You can configure action scenarios that the system performs automatically when an event occurs, for example, sends a notification, records data, creates a command, and so on. Notification management You define which events trigger notifications, who they are sent to, and which handling algorithm is used.

The “Control room” module helps the system respond to events automatically. It uses event-handling algorithms: predefined sequences of actions that run when certain conditions are met. For example, you can configure the system to: — immediately notify the operator and mark the event as critical when speed or temperature is exceeded — create a task for the dispatcher and send the driver a reminder in case of a long idle period — record the arrival time and send an SMS to the customer when the vehicle enters the customer’s geofence Creating an algorithm Go to the “Algorithms” section in the top interface menu 2. Create a new algorithm On the “List” tab, click the “Add” button . The builder workspace opens 3. Assemble the algorithm from blocks In the workspace you can drag blocks and arrange them into a scenario. Each block is a separate step that the system performs when the event is triggered. Available blocks: Start block: the starting point of the algorithm Text: displays a message or comment Command: a system action (for example, sending a notification) Command template: a ready-made action for reuse Webhook: sends an HTTP request to an external system. The block lets you pass event data to a third-party service, for example a CRM, a dispatch system, or a corporate application Condition: a logical check (for example, if the temperature exceeds a threshold) Choice: a fork with several action options End: completes the algorithm Additional blocks may also be available, depending on the system configuration. 4. Arrange the blocks and connect them An algorithm usually starts with the “Start block”, followed by condition checks and actions, and ends with the “End” block. Connect the blocks by dragging branches between them. For example, branches are set from the “Condition” block to the “Text” block: “Yes”: if the condition is met “No”: if the condition is not met Place the Webhook block in the branch where data must be sent to an external system. If the request must be sent regardless of the check result, add a separate Webhook block to both branches. At this stage only the structure of the algorithm is defined. Parameter values (conditions, message texts, request parameters, and other settings) are specified later, when you link the algorithm to a notification. 5. Save the algorithm When the diagram is ready, click “Accept”. In the window that appears, enter a name for the algorithm and click “OK”. The algorithm is saved in the list and becomes available for use. Example of a simple algorithm Task: record an event if the cargo temperature exceeds the allowed value. How to build the algorithm: 1. Add the “Start block” 2. Add the “Condition” block, which checks that the temperature is above normal The “Temperature” parameter and the threshold are set later, when linking to a notification. 3. From the “Condition” block, place “Text” blocks and draw the “Yes” and “No” branches to them 4. Complete the algorithm with the “End” block and make sure all blocks are connected This is a basic algorithm that can be used as a foundation for automatic event handling. A created algorithm does not run on its own. To make it work, you need to link it to a notification. You can read how to do this in the next article .

This article explains how to set up algorithms to work through notifications. You will learn: — how to link an algorithm to a notification so that it runs automatically when events occur — how to create a notification with an algorithm for manual event generation For an algorithm to start working and respond to events, it must be linked to a notification. For linking to work, the “Notifications” module must be enabled in the contract. Linking an algorithm to an event Such an algorithm runs automatically when the conditions are met and arrives in the “Control room”. 1. In the top panel, click the icon and open “Contract settings”. Go to the “Notifications” tab. 2. Click “Add” to create a new notification 3. Link the algorithm In the notification settings window, click “Algorithm linking” Select the algorithm you need from the list Click the algorithm; its diagram with blocks opens 4. Configure the algorithm blocks Double-click the block you need Fill in the text and select event tags Click “OK” How to create a tag for a block Tags help you quickly understand the essence of an event and visually highlight it in the list. If the tag you need does not exist: 1. In the “Tag” field, click 2. In the tags window, click to add a new tag to the list 3. Enter the tag name and select a color 4. Save; the tag appears in the list and becomes available for selection Configuring the Webhook block The Webhook block passes event information from PILOT to an external system, for example a CRM, a dispatch system, or a corporate application. The request is sent when algorithm execution reaches this block. For more on how Webhook notifications work and how to configure them, see this article . If the algorithm uses a Webhook block: 1. Select the Webhook block in the diagram 2. Double-click it to open its settings 3. Click the edit icon next to the block name 4. Fill in the parameters in the Webhook Details window URL Specify the address of the external system to which PILOT should send the data. You need to get the address from the administrator or developer of the receiving system. Header Specify the request headers. By default, data is sent in JSON format: [ "ContentType: application/json" ] Change the headers only if the receiving system requires a different data format or additional parameters. Body Specify the data to send. By default, the following template is used: { "agent_id": "%AGENTID%", "vehiclenumber": "%VEHNUM%", "ts": "%TS%", "lat": "%LAT%", "lon": "%LON%", "speed": "%SPEED%", "data": "%DATA%", "zone": "%ZONE%", "driver": "%DRIVER%" } Instead of the variables enclosed in % signs, the system automatically substitutes information from the event. For example, %SPEED% is replaced with the object’s speed, and %VEHNUM% with the vehicle number. You can change the request body: remove unneeded fields, add your own fields, or use other available variables. Keep the JSON format valid: field_name : %VARIABLE% If the JSON structure or a variable is written incorrectly, the external system may not receive or process the request. Allowed variables Variable What it passes %ACCOUNTID% Account ID %AGENTID% Object ID %VEHNUM% Vehicle number %TS% Timestamp %DATETIME% Date and time %LAT% Latitude %LON% Longitude %SPEED% Speed %ODO% Mileage (from the sensor) %DATA% Notification data %ZONE% Geofence %ZONE_ID% ID of the first geofence %ZONE_NAME% Name of the first geofence %DRIVER% Driver %MAXSPEED% Maximum speed (for speeding notifications) %DUR% Duration of the speeding %SPEEDLIMIT% Set speed limit (Speed control) The set of available variables may depend on the notification type. For example, the variables %MAXSPEED%, %DUR%, and %SPEEDLIMIT% are intended for speeding notifications. After filling in the parameters, click “Save”, then confirm the block configuration with the “OK” button. If different branches of the algorithm use different Webhook blocks, configure each of them separately. Configuring the event processing window You can configure how the event processing window looks for the operator: In the algorithm linking window, click “Settings” 2. Click to add elements: What you can configure: Element type: the kind of block (for example, plaintext is plain text) Title: the block name Text: information for the operator For example: 1. Add a row of the plaintext type 2. In the “Title” field, write what this block is (for example: “Event information”) 3. In the “Text” field, add the information the operator should see (for example: “Check the temperature in the cargo body and contact the driver”). To add a section with vehicle information, click the car icon. A new block of the vehicle type appears, where you can set the title and text. 1 — Add vehicle information. To add a section with driver data, click the driver’s license icon. A new block of the driver type appears. In this block you can set the title and text. 2 — Add driver information After configuring, click “OK”; the operator will see the form exactly in this form when processing the event. Completing the notification setup In the “Notification settings” window, specify: Notification name Object Notification type: Control room (GARM) Group Notification conditions (for example, the “Temperature” parameter and its threshold) 2. Click “Save” 3. The notification with the linked algorithm appears in the list and is sent to the “Control room” when the conditions are met Algorithm for manual event generation Manual generation is needed when an event does not arrive automatically, for example, for non-routine situations, testing, or an operator recording an event manually. How to create a notification for manual generation 1. Open “Contract settings” and select the “Notifications” tab 2. On the “Notifications” tab, click 3. In the notification settings, specify: 1 — Notification type “Control room” (GARM) 2 — Notification for manual generation only Object Notification name Notification type: Control room (GARM) Group The “Manual generation only” check box 4. Click “Algorithm linking” 5. In the algorithms window that opens, select the one you want to link to the notification and click “OK” 5. Save the notification How to generate an event manually 1. Select the object in the main list 2. Right-click it and select “Generate event” 3. Select the notification type for manual generation and enter the event text 4. The event appears on the “Control room” panel and is processed according to the algorithm

The event history helps you understand what happened, on which object, and exactly how the system responded. To view the event history: 1. Go to the “Algorithms” section in the top menu and select the “History” tab Specify a date or date range and click “Search”; a list of events appears below If you need to save the history to files, use the buttons: 1 — Save the history to PDF 2 — Save the history to XLSX If you need to show only unprocessed events, select the “Unprocessed” check box 3. Click the arrow next to an event to see the details The event shows: Date and time of the event The object on which it occurred The group the event belongs to Event text Operator: the user who processed or confirmed the event Processing date: when the operator actually processed the event Algorithm diagram To the right of the event list, a diagram of the algorithm that was run for the selected event is displayed. The diagram shows: algorithm blocks: the steps the system performs algorithm branches: possible ways the scenario can develop The diagram helps you understand which steps the system performed and which path the algorithm took when processing the event. Example diagram: This algorithm contains the following blocks: Start: the beginning of the algorithm, the moment the event occurs Condition: a condition check. For example: “speed 90 km/h for longer than 10 seconds”. Two branches come out of the condition: Yes: the condition was met No: the condition was not met Text / Command blocks: system actions End: completion of event processing The blue line shows which path the algorithm took. For example: Start → Condition → (Yes) → Text → End. Gray lines are branches that were not triggered in this event.

Module panel When a notification with a linked algorithm is triggered, the event immediately appears in the interface, in the operator’s workspace panel for event processing. The “Control room” panel is located at the bottom of the “Main” section interface. To expand the panel, click the arrow . The panel shows a list of all events that came in through notifications and are waiting for the operator’s response. Top part The top part of the panel helps you find the events you need. It provides: Event groups: a filter by type (speed, temperature, geofence, and so on) Search : search by object or event text Refresh : manually refreshes the list Additional actions : — Event processing interval: the time during which an event is considered current and available for processing. Select the interval you need from the list to define how long an event is displayed in the list before it is automatically moved to the “unprocessed” status. — Page size: the number of events displayed on one page — Grouping: combines identical events of one object into a single row for convenience. — Processed: select the check box to show processed events. By default, only unprocessed events are displayed. Event table Each row is an object with a current event or a group of events. Main columns: Date: the time of the last event Object: the object name. An address or zone may be displayed under it Stage: the current step of the algorithm Operator: who took the event into work Event: The group the event belongs to A red circle with a number shows how many events are not yet processed Text: the standard event description Alternative text: a custom description from the notification settings (if set) To the left of the row there is an arrow that expands the list of all events within the group. How to start processing an event 1. When a notification is triggered, the event appears in the list on the panel 2. Click the row; the event is displayed on the map 3. Expand the row and select the event you need 4. Click: “Start” to process the event “Skip” if the event does not require processing “Event processing” window After you click “Start”, a step-by-step processing window opens; it follows the logic of your algorithm. In the top part: Event ID: internal number Address: the place of the event. You can copy it by clicking Event text: description Event information: a hint for the operator from the algorithm Below: Comment: what the operator did about the event If the algorithm contains additional steps, the following may appear: drop-down lists for selecting a reason or status the “Next step” button: moves to the next block of the algorithm Completing processing On the last step of the algorithm there may be two buttons: Yes: confirms the event (a violation occurred, the action was taken) No: an alternative result (false alarm, no action required) After you choose: — the algorithm ends — the event is considered processed — the result is saved in the history If the algorithm has no fork, a “Finish” button appears instead of “Yes / No”. How to work with the event processing window In the processing window, click the map icon ; a built-in map opens at the bottom. On the map you will see: the object’s position at the time of the event the track of movement before and after the event the address and coordinates Click the icon in the processing window to open an additional panel with detailed data on the object and the event. It has three blocks: 1. Sensors — sensor values at the time of the event — current values now 2. Processed events — the date of previous events for this object — which operators processed them — processing time, group, and event text 3. Task information — task number and status — time of status changes — route and actual times On this panel the operator sees the full context of the event without leaving the processing window.

You can configure how events are displayed in the “Control room”: set groups, colors, and processing statuses. 1. Go to “Contract settings” 2. Open the “Control room” tab In the interface it may currently be called GARM, which is the module’s former name. Event group settings On the left is the list of event groups coming from the “Control room” (for example: Observation, Arming/Disarming, RFID Antenna, and others). Each row is a separate event group. For it you can configure: Group color: select a color from the list. The color helps you identify the event type, for example, blue for observation, red for alarms “Alarm” type: select the check box if events of this group should be considered alarms The trash icon deletes a group if it is no longer needed. How to add an event group: Click the “Add” button at the bottom of the event list Select a color for the new group If necessary, select the “Alarm” type After saving, the new group immediately appears in the list and starts being used in the “Control room”. Stage color settings On the right you choose the color used to show the event state. The color helps you understand what is currently happening with the event. In progress: the event is being processed Unprocessed: a new event Processed: events that the algorithm and the operator have already handled Unprocessed (timer expired): the event was not processed in time To set a color, select it from the drop-down list.

The “Climate” module is designed to monitor temperature and humidity on monitoring objects where temperature and humidity control is important, for example, residential premises, warehouses, offices, and cold rooms. In standard mode of the “Climate” module, you can: — view the current sensor values — see the date and time of the last update — track changes in readings — display sensors on the room plan When the Velavu integration is connected, the “Climate” module can also be used for indoor positioning — tracking objects inside buildings. In this mode, the module displays Velavu objects, their location on the plan, status, and movement history.

The “Climate” module helps you monitor temperature and humidity at monitored objects. In it you can group sensors into a structure of rooms, view their current values, follow updates, and display sensors on an object plan. In this article we will cover: What to do before you start How the module interface is organized How to create a room How to add nested elements How to add a sensor How to work with sensors in the list How to upload a room plan How to place sensors on the plan Which actions are available for a room Before you start For the “Climate” module to work correctly, temperature or humidity sensors must be set up in advance on the monitored objects. The module works only with sensors that are already added to the system and linked to monitored objects. Therefore, before you start, make sure that: 1. A monitored object has been created 2. A temperature or humidity sensor is set up on the object Example Suppose you want to monitor the temperature in a residential space. Then: 1. First, create an object named Home in the monitoring system. To learn how to create a monitored object, read here . 2. Then add a temperature sensor to it. To learn how to set up a sensor on an object, read here . 3. After that, open the “Climate” module and link the sensor to a room Module interface The module interface is divided into two main parts: List of rooms and sensors On the left is the main workspace with a list of: Names of buildings, floors, and rooms Sensors linked to each room The current value of each sensor Time of the last update A mini-chart of reading changes Tools are located at the top of the list: Search: a field for quickly finding the object or sensor you need Filter: to select items by conditions “Add” button: to add a new room Refresh button: to refresh the data Room plan If an SVG plan has been uploaded for the room, the plan with sensor markers is displayed on the right. How to work with the module 1. Create a room To start monitoring the climate, you need to create a structure: a building, a floor, or a room Go to the “Climate” section 2. Click the button at the top of the list 3. In the window that appears, enter the room name 4. Click OK The new room appears in the list. You can now work with it through the context menu. If you want to change a room you created: 1. Right-click it 2. In the menu, select “Edit” 3. In the window that opens, change the name 4. If necessary, select the room type: building, floor, room 5. Click “Add” 2. Add nested elements If your room consists of several zones, you can make the structure more detailed. For example, add floors to a building and rooms to a floor. 1. Right-click the room you need in the list 2. In the menu, select “Add room” 3. Specify the name of the new element 4. Select the room type: building, floor, or room 5. Click “Add” The new element appears inside the selected room. You can repeat this process to build the structure you need. 3. Add a sensor After creating a room, you need to link a sensor to it: 1. Select the room you need in the list 2. Right-click and select “Add sensor” 3. A settings window opens where you need to select: Monitored object: the object the sensor is linked to Sensor: the temperature or humidity sensor you need from the list 4. Click “Add” After saving, the sensor appears in the “Climate” module list. It displays: Name: the sensor name in the system Current value: the temperature or humidity right now Update time: when data was last received Mini-chart : how the value changed over time If a plan has been uploaded , the sensor is also displayed on it. How to work with sensors in the list Sensor tooltip If you hover the cursor over a sensor in the list, a tooltip appears. It shows: sensor name sensor ID sensor type current value current status The following statuses can be used for sensors: In range: the value is within the allowed range Out of range: the value has gone beyond the allowed limits Offline: no current data is arriving from the sensor Mini-chart A mini-chart of the sensor’s operation and reading changes may be displayed next to the sensor in the list. It helps you quickly see how values changed over time. If you hover the cursor over the chart, you can see a tooltip with additional information, for example, the value at a specific point and the time the reading changed. How to delete a sensor 1. Right-click the sensor 2. Select “Delete sensor” 3. Confirm the deletion How to upload a room plan A room plan is an SVG file with a plan of your object. After uploading the plan and adding sensors, you can: — see sensors directly on the plan — compare values between rooms and see the temperature difference in different zones — monitor the situation visually How to upload 1. Select the room you need in the list 2. Right-click and select “Upload SVG” 3. Select the SVG file with the room plan 4. Specify the width and height of the plan; these are the dimensions at which the plan is displayed in the interface 5. Save After that, the plan appears on the right side of the module window. How to place sensors on the plan After you upload an SVG plan, the added sensors appear on it automatically. You can drag the sensors with the mouse and place them according to their actual location in the room. When you hover the mouse over a sensor on the plan, a tooltip with its name and current value appears. Room actions menu To open the actions menu, right-click the room. Through this menu you can: Edit the element Add room: create a nested structure element Upload plan: add an SVG file so that the plan appears on the right side of the window Add sensor: connect a temperature or humidity sensor Delete element: delete the room

Velavu is an indoor positioning system that lets you track the location of objects inside buildings. It uses fixed positioning points — anchors — and mobile tags to determine the location of equipment, vehicles, assets, or personnel on a building or floor plan. The Velavu integration with PILOT lets you work with this data in the system interface. With the Velavu integration in PILOT, you can: — load the structure of sites, buildings, and floors from Velavu — see the location of objects inside buildings — open detailed information about devices — track movement history

The Velavu integration is configured at the partner account level through configuration parameters. Integration setup is available only to users with main administrator rights. If you do not have the appropriate access level, contact support. 1. In the admin panel, go to the “Partners” section 2. Double-click the partner you need; the partner card opens 3. Go to the “Configuration” tab 4. Click the “Add” button 5. In the drop-down list, select the Velavu key. In the parameter value, paste the Velavu configuration in JSON format. Example of a Velavu JSON configuration [ { "broker": "iot.velavu.com", "port": "8883", "customer_id": "YOUR_CUSTOMER_ID", "api_token": "YOUR_API_TOKEN", "cert": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
YOUR_CERTIFICATE
-----END CERTIFICATE-----", "key": "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----" } ] Parameter Description broker Velavu MQTT broker address port Connection port customer_id Customer ID in the Velavu system api_token Velavu API access token cert SSL certificate for the connection key SSL private key You obtain all the data (customer_id, api_token, certificate, and key) from your Velavu account. 6. Save the configuration. After that, the integration becomes available for the accounts that belong to this partner

With the Velavu integration in PILOT, you can track the location of objects inside buildings in real time: which floor, room, or zone equipment and personnel are in. In this article we will cover: How to switch to Velavu mode How to get started with Velavu How to synchronize How to interact with devices How to view device details Object and device menu Velavu geofences How to switch to Velavu mode After the Velavu integration is connected, the “Climate” module lets you switch between two modes: Standard — the regular “Climate” module mode for working with temperature and humidity sensors Velavu — the mode that displays Velavu objects 1. Open the “Climate” module 2. On the “Climate” tab, use the drop-down list to switch the mode from “Standard” to “Velavu” 3. The interface switches to Velavu mode In Velavu mode, the Velavu object tree is displayed instead of the usual temperature and humidity sensors. Each element in the tree usually shows: the object name, for example, Velavu-00Q6N the type, for example: — ANCHOR — anchor — TAG — tag — Device — device In Velavu mode, the following are available at the top of the window: Filter — to select the elements you need Search — to quickly find a device, floor, or site Synchronization button — to load or update the structure from Velavu Add button — lets you manually add a room if you need to extend the structure How to get started with Velavu For Velavu objects to appear in the “Climate” module, you first need to prepare the objects in the system. 1. Create a monitoring object. To learn how to create an object, read the separate article . 2. In the object card, enter the object identifier from the Velavu system 3. After that, you can configure the object further, for example: — select an icon — specify a color — fill in other parameters 4. Run synchronization Once the objects are prepared, go to the “Climate” module and synchronize the structure. Synchronizing the Velavu structure Synchronization is needed to load the object structure from Velavu and display it in the “Climate” module: 1. Open the “Climate” module 2. Switch to Velavu mode 3. Click the synchronization button 4. The system loads buildings, floors, and devices from the Velavu API After synchronization, the entire structure appears in the object tree, grouped by account, building, and floor. How to interact with Velavu objects If you click an object in the tree on the left, the corresponding object on the plan is highlighted. If you click an object on the plan, it is automatically selected in the object list. Which objects are displayed in Velavu The module can display different types of objects: Anchors — fixed reference points used to calculate the position of other devices Tags — tags that are usually attached to equipment, people, or other objects. Once the anchors are configured, their position is calculated automatically. Proximity Tags — tags that are detected within the radius of another object Color coding of Velavu objects Velavu objects are displayed on the plan as colored circles. The color indicates the object type and its status: Color Object type Description Blue Anchor (Anchor ) Fixed positioning point installed in a room Green Tag (Tag) Moving object — equipment, vehicle, or personnel Yellow Proximity Tags (Proximity Tags) Tag located within the range of another object Red Offline The object is not transmitting data or is outside the coverage area Tooltip on hover If you hover over an object in the list or on the plan, a tooltip with brief information about the object appears. The tooltip shows: Name — the object name in the system Agent ID — the internal object identifier Device ID — the Velavu device identifier Location type — the object placement type Coordinates — the current coordinates of the object Site — the name of the site the object belongs to Floor — the floor where the object is located Status — the current state of the device: online or offline This tooltip helps you get the main information about an object without opening the device card. Viewing device details A detailed card with full information is available for each Velavu device. To open it, click the view icon next to the object in the tree. The device card opens as a separate window with several tabs: Basic information This tab shows general information about the device: where it is located, what it is attached to, and its status. Device name — the device name in the Velavu system, for example, Velavu-Sp8mv Device ID — the unique device identifier, for example, Sp8mv Site — the name of the site where the device is installed, for example, GARGASH Floor — the floor where the device is located, for example, Level 1 - GR001 Connection status — the current state of the device: online or offline Below is the “Assignment” block, which may show information about the asset: Asset name — the asset the device is attached to Asset group — the group the asset belongs to Asset category — the asset category Operation — the current action or state of the asset At the bottom of the tab, the following field is displayed: Last update — the date and time when data was last received from the device Location The “Location” tab shows data about the device location. Here you can see: Floor name — the floor where the device is located Site name — the site where the device is placed Location type — the way the device is placed Latitude — the current latitude value Longitude — the current longitude value Nearest device ID — the identifier of the nearest device Distance to device — the distance to the nearest device Device status The “Device status” tab shows the current technical state of the device. Battery status This block may show: Charge level — the battery charge percentage, for example, 90% Battery charging — whether the device is connected to a charger Connection This block shows: Connection status — online or offline RSSI — signal level Gateway ID — the identifier of the gateway the device is connected through Signal level — connection quality Movement and activity In this block you can see: Motion detection — whether the object is moving or stationary Last activity — the date and time of the device s last activity Environment This tab shows environmental sensor data if the device supports measuring temperature, humidity, or pressure. Here you can see: Temperature — the current value in °C Humidity — the current value in % Pressure — the current value in kPa Below is the “History charts” block. If data is available, charts of temperature, humidity, and pressure changes are displayed here. Above the charts you can select the viewing period: 1h — 1 hour, 6h — 6 hours, 1d — 1 day, 7d — 7 days, 30d — 30 days, All — the entire available period Assignment The “Assignment” tab shows which asset the device is associated with. Here you can usually see: Asset name — the asset the device is attached to Asset group — the group the asset belongs to Asset category — the asset category Operation — the current action or state of the asset If the asset data is not filled in, the fields may show N/A. Technical data The “Technical data” tab shows additional service information about the device. Depending on the device, the following may be available here: Firmware / model Beacon interval Heartbeat frequency State update frequency Temperature and humidity update frequency Beacon transmit power Site ID Floor ID Velavu object menu A context menu with additional actions is available for Velavu floors and sites. To open the object actions menu, right-click the Velavu object. Through this menu you can: Edit — change the name and type of the room Add room — create a nested element of the structure Show anchors — show the fixed positioning points on the object plan. Anchors are hidden by default. To show the anchors, select “Show anchors” in the menu. They will appear on the plan and in the list. To hide the anchors, select “Hide anchors” in the menu. Add object — link a Velavu monitoring object to a room Delete element — remove a room from the structure Velavu device menu For an individual Velavu device, the following action is available in the context menu: Delete object This action removes the link between the device and the Velavu room. Velavu geofences Velavu geofences are loaded into the system automatically from Velavu. You do not need to create them manually in PILOT. It is enough to configure the sites and buildings in Velavu and then click the synchronization button in Velavu mode in the “Climate” module. The system will automatically import the geofences, the structure of sites and floors, and the related devices. After that, the Velavu geofences will appear in the “Geofences” section in a separate folder.

On the “History” tab, you can view the history of Velavu objects for a selected period. You can: — see where an object was at a specific moment — see which room it was in — trace the movement of the object on the map How to open the Velavu history 1. Go to the “History” tab 2. In the “View” field, select Velavu mode 3. Specify: Period from Period to 4. In the “Objects” field, select one or more Velavu objects whose history you want to view After that, records for the selected objects appear in the table below. The following columns are usually displayed for each record: Name — the Velavu object name RFID — if RFID data is available Type — the object type, for example: Anchor (ANCHOR) or tag (TAG) Date — the date and time of the record Building — the building the record relates to Floor — the floor where the object was located Duration — how long the object stayed in this state or place Sensor — related sensor data, if any Actions — buttons for viewing and playback You can customize which columns are displayed: 1. In the header of any column, click the arrow . A menu with column settings appears, where you can: • Sort the data in ascending or descending order • Choose which columns to show on the screen 2. To choose which columns to show: Click “Columns” — a list of parameters available for display in the list opens Select the check boxes next to the parameters you want to see What you can do in the history 1. View records by object The history is grouped by each selected object. For each object, you can expand the list of records and view its history over time. 2. View the object on the map If you select a record in the list, a map is displayed on the right. On the map, you will see the position of the object at the time of the record 3. Play back movements Next to each device there is a player — a play button and a slider. With the player, you can see how the device moved around the site over time 4. View the device card Next to each record there is an icon . Click it to open the Velavu device card. The card opens with exactly the data that was present when the record was created.

The “RFID tags” module is designed for creating and managing RFID tags, which are used for automatic identification of objects in the monitoring system. Tags help the system determine which object a vehicle interacted with. For example, they can be used to determine which container a garbage truck serviced or which checkpoint a vehicle visited. In the module, you can: — add RFID tags and combine them into groups — check the time of the last read — view the location of a tag on the map — view the read history How RFID tags work RFID requires two elements: — RFID reader — a device on the vehicle that detects nearby tags — RFID tag — a device with a unique identifier, installed on a container, trailer, equipment, or another object When a tag comes within range of the reader: 1. The RFID reader on the vehicle detects the tag 2. The reader receives the tag s unique identifier and transmits it to PILOT 3. PILOT looks for a tag with this identifier in the RFID tag directory 4. If the tag is found, the system updates the information about its last read 5. If automatic actions are defined for the tag or its associated object, the system performs them Where RFID tags are used Automatic trailer linking An RFID tag is installed on the trailer and a reader on the tractor unit. When the trailer comes within range of the reader, PILOT recognizes the tag and can automatically link the trailer to the vehicle. Route control RFID or BLE tags are installed at checkpoints: at stops, warehouses, company premises, and other locations. When a vehicle is near a tag, PILOT records the visit to the checkpoint. Container servicing control RFID tags are installed on containers, and readers on garbage trucks or other service machinery. On each read, PILOT saves information about the container, the time and place of service, and the vehicle that performed the work. Vehicle identification RFID tags help recognize vehicles when entering company premises, passing checkpoints, and performing production operations. Driver identification A personal RFID tag can be assigned to a driver. After the read, PILOT identifies the driver and can link a trip, events, or completed work to them.

Before you start, install an RFID reader, connect it to the tracker, and set up the transmission of identifiers to PILOT. 1. Install the hardware 1. Install the RFID reader on a vehicle or other machinery 2. Connect the reader to the tracker that transmits data to PILOT 3. Attach RFID tags to the objects you need to recognize. Tags can be attached, for example, to containers, trailers, equipment, checkpoints, and stationary and movable objects 2. Configure the RFID reader in PILOT 1. Add an RFID sensor to the object s sensors 2. Select the device field in which the reader transmits the tag identifier 3. Save the settings After configuration, PILOT starts receiving identifiers from the hardware and looking for matching records in the RFID tag directory. If the reader transmits an identifier that is not in the RFID tag directory, the system cannot match it with an existing record. Such a tag may be displayed as Unknown . Once an RFID tag with the corresponding identifier is added to the system, PILOT will recognize it correctly on subsequent reads. 4. Add the RFID tags used on your objects to the directory. For each tag, specify its unique ID and other required parameters. After saving, PILOT will be able to match the identifiers received from the reader with the tags you created. For detailed instructions, see the article “How to manage RFID tags” . RFID in the object card The object card has an RFID field. In it, you can specify the identifier of the tag associated with this object. For example, if the monitoring object is a container with an RFID tag, enter the identifier of the installed tag in the field. PILOT uses this information in the RFID module and when generating reports .

In the “RFID tags” module, you can add and edit tags, combine them into groups, search for the records you need, and load data from Excel. How to add an RFID tag To create a new RFID tag: 1. Go to the “RFID tags” tab 2. Click the “Add” button The RFID tag creation card opens. Fill in the required fields: ID — the unique identifier of the RFID tag. It is usually entered manually, using the identifier that the RFID reader transmits when it reads the tag. In some cases, the ID may be assigned automatically after the hardware reads the RFID tag for the first time. Name — the name of the RFID tag under which it will be displayed in the system Group — the group the tag belongs to Description — additional information about the tag Latitude and longitude — approximate coordinates of the RFID tag location. For example, if the RFID tag is attached to a container site, a checkpoint, or another stationary object, you can save its coordinates in the system Fixed tag — enable this parameter if the tag is in a permanent location and does not move. A stationary RFID tag can be linked to a geofence , to a route point , or to a bus stop . In this case, PILOT will take the tag read into account when determining visits to these zones 3. Click “Save”. After saving, the tag appears in the general list How to create an RFID tag group If the group you need does not exist in the system yet, you can create it when adding or editing a tag. 1. In the “Group” field, enter the name of the new group 2. Fill in the other tag parameters 3. Click “Save” The new group is created automatically and becomes available when you add subsequent RFID tags. How to edit an RFID tag 1. Double-click the tag in the list 2. Change the required parameters 3. Click “Save” How to find an RFID tag To search, use the group filter or the search bar. 1 — Search by group Select a group above the list. After you select it, the table is updated and only the records that belong to this group remain. 2 — Search by name or ID Enter a known value in the search bar. Only the records that match the query remain in the list. To show all tags again, clear the search bar. Toolbar commands The top panel of the module provides commands for creating, updating, importing, exporting, and displaying RFID tags. Add — create an RFID tag Export to Excel — save the tag list to an XLSX file Import from Excel — load RFID tags from an XLSX file to add or update the tag list. Before importing, make sure the file structure matches the Excel template Download Excel template — download a file template for importing RFID tags. Fill in the required fields in the template and save the file, then use “Import from Excel” and upload the completed file Refresh — refresh the RFID tag list without reloading the page Icon color settings — configure the color display of RFID tags on the map depending on when the latest data was received Show on map — display the selected RFID tags on the map. Before using it, select one or more tags in the list Clear map — remove all displayed RFID tags from the map RFID tag actions Additional actions are available for RFID tags in the list. Show on map — view the last known location of the RFID tag on the map Tag history — view the usage history of the RFID tag Delete tag — delete the RFID tag from the system

In the “RFID tags” module, you can check the last read, show a tag on the map, and view its usage history. How to check the last read When a vehicle detects an RFID tag, PILOT automatically updates the information in its row. The list shows: 1 — Updated: the date and time of the last information update 2 — Last update: how much time has passed since the read 3 — Vehicle: the monitoring object that last read the tag The vehicle appears in the row after the tag has actually been read. Physical contact between the reader and the tag is not required. It is enough for the tag to be within range of the hardware. How to show one tag on the map 1. Find the actions menu in the tag row 2. Select “Show on map” The map moves to the last known location of the tag and shows a marker. Click the marker to open a tooltip. It shows: — the date and time of the last update — the tag name — the tag ID — coordinates, which you can copy — the address To close the tooltip, click the cross in its upper-right corner or select another marker. How to show several tags 1. Select one or more tags in the list 2. On the toolbar, click “Show on map” Markers for the selected tags appear on the map. To remove all markers, click “Clear map” . How to view the history of an RFID tag 1. Open the actions menu in the tag row 2. Select “Tag history” For each read, the following are displayed: — the vehicle that read the tag — date and time — the coordinates of the read How to configure the marker color The marker color shows how much time has passed since the latest data was received. The following rules apply by default: — green — data was received no more than four hours ago — red — more than four hours have passed since data was received The color helps you quickly spot tags whose information has not been updated for a long time. To configure marker colors: 1. Click “Icon color settings” on the toolbar 2. In the “RFID tag icon colors” window, click 3. Add a rule and specify for it: — the icon color — the comparison condition — the time in hours 4. Click “Save” — the rules are applied

Statistics are displayed for the last 24 hours. Open the Dashboard tab. Select an object from the list. Select a date. View the vehicle info block. Reports are not provided in the Analytics module. Important! Depending on the connected modules, for example Eco-driving, the PTM module, or geofence violations, these values will also be shown in charts on the corresponding topics. From the geofence block, you can jump to the “Online” tab, where the vehicles located in the specified geofences are highlighted in the object tree. How do I display the objects? Click the bar representing the geofence. Right-click to open the menu. “Show vehicles on the main map”. • Only the objects located in this zone will be highlighted in the object tree. Return to the module in the usual way. In this example, all 6 objects that the system highlighted for this geofence are displayed. Data refresh button. Select a template A user can create their own profile and set it as the default. The system administrator can create a profile and set it as the default for a partner account. In this case, all users will see this profile as the default profile. Create a template After selecting the additional parameters, click “Save as new”. Right-click a chart, and the system will offer several reports to generate. To return to Analytics, click “Back”. Generate reports on the corresponding topics, for example, reports related to mileage, fuel consumption, and machinery operation. For example, for the Mileage chart you can generate the following reports: Mileage report. Mileage report No. 2. Mileage with drivers. The reports will be generated on the regular “Reports” tab with all the details on duration, distance, address, and other fields. To return to the Analytics module from the Reports section, go to the Dashboard tab in the usual way.

The engine blocking module lets you remotely block and unblock a vehicle through the system. For the function to work, a special blocking relay must be installed on the vehicle. How to connect the module Configuration is performed in the admin panel at the contract level. 1. Open the contract card 2. Right-click to open the contract menu and select “Edit” 3. Go to the “Modules” tab 4. Enable the engine blocking module 4. Save the changes Command configuration The module can be linked to any of your command templates: 1. In the admin panel, go to the contract card 2. Go to the “Module settings” tab 3. Select the engine blocking module 4. In the “Configs” block, add a configuration: arm_template_id — the ID of the command template for blocking the engine disarm_template_id — the ID of the command template for unblocking the engine In the “Value” field, enter the ID of the command template you created. 5. Save the contract settings After that: — when you click “Block”, the system sends the command from the arm_template_id template — when you click “Unblock”, it sends the command from the disarm_template_id template How to block or unblock the engine 1. In the user account, select the object you need 2. Right-click the object to open its context menu 3. Select “Block” or “Unblock” 4. Enter the contract password to confirm and click the corresponding button After confirmation, the command is sent to the device. The contract s Master password, specified in its card, is used for confirmation.

The “Scales” module automatically determines the weight of cargo using sensors installed on vehicles. With the module, you can: — monitor the weight of vehicles — add and configure weighing checkpoints — see the history of all weighings — keep records of transported materials — export weighing data for reports How it works 1. Scale sensors that transmit data to PILOT are installed on the vehicle 2. A weighing checkpoint is created on the map 3. When an empty vehicle crosses the checkpoint, PILOT records the current weight 4. After a material, for example crushed stone, sand, or grain, is loaded, the object crosses the checkpoint again 5. The system records the new weight and calculates the cargo mass How to add scales 1. Go to the “Main” section and select the “Scales” tab 2. Click the “Add” button 3. Fill in the fields in the window that appears: ID — the unique identifier of the scales Scales name Description — additional information about the scales Latitude and longitude — the coordinates of the scales location 4. Click “Save” The new scales are added to the scales list. If the new scales do not appear in the list, click “Refresh”. To change the scales parameters, double-click the scales in the list with the left mouse button — a window with the parameters opens. Edit the required fields and save the changes. Weighing history To view the weighing history for specific scales, click the “History” icon in the scales list. Here you will see data on all weighings with information about vehicles and cargo: Vehicle number Vehicle type First time and second time — entry and exit time First weight and second weight — the weight before and after weighing Cargo type, for example, “Crushed stone 5-20” Client name To save the weighing information, click the “Export” button — the data is saved in CSV format.

The “Geofences” module is designed for territorial control of monitoring objects. With it, you can: — track when an object enters or leaves a specific zone — monitor idle time in a zone and receive notifications when the allowed time is exceeded — get reports on the movements and actions of objects in specified areas What is a geofence? A geofence is a designated area on the map that you create to monitor the movement of objects. A geofence can have any shape: Polygon — for example, the territory of a company or an entire city Circle — a zone with an arbitrary radius Line — for example, a specific street or road section You can configure automatic notifications about entering or leaving a geofence, and view reports on all geofence-related events in the “Reports” section. To create and work with geofences, you must have the appropriate access rights .

To create a geofence: In the “Main” section, select the “Geofences” tab 2. Create a zone group For convenient organization, you can group geofences by region or type: Click the group icon Enter the group name and click “Save” 3. Select the zone type and add the zone: Polygon — mark the vertices of the polygon on the map Circle — hold down the left mouse button and drag to set the radius of the circle. You can change the radius by dragging the markers on the circumference. You can move the zone by dragging the center Line — mark two or more points on the map to build the segment or route you need 4. Enter the zone name and choose a color for it 5. Click “Save” — the geofence appears in the list

Linking a geofence to an object lets you automatically track its movements, monitor idle time and speed, and receive notifications about violations. How to configure: 1. Open the settings of the zone you need 2. Link objects to the geofence Select the check boxes next to the objects that should be associated with this geofence. The system will track their movements relative to the selected zone and apply all the specified parameters to them. 3. Configure additional parameters: Idle control — specify the time in minutes after which staying in the zone is considered idle time. For example, if you specify 15 minutes, the system records an idle period if the object stays in the zone longer than this time. If you specify 0, idle time in this zone is not counted (this is the default value). Idle data can be viewed in the dedicated idle reports and in summary reports Speed control — set a speed limit for objects within this geofence Zone type — choose whether the zone is a working zone or a restricted zone: — working geofence — an area where the object should be and perform its tasks (for example, a warehouse, a construction site, a route) — restricted geofence — an area the object must not enter (for example, private property, hazardous or closed areas, military facilities) Alert type — configure the alert type in this zone: — idle in zone — the system sends an alert if the object stays in the zone longer than the set time — border crossing — the system sends an alert when the object enters or leaves the geofence — idle in zone and border crossing — the system sends an alert on either of these events Recalculate geofences for (number of days) If you changed the geofence parameters or have just created a new one, you can recalculate the events for this zone for a past period (for example, the last 7 days). To do this, select the “Recalculate geofences for” check box and choose the number of days. The system recalculates all events (entries, exits, idle periods, and so on) for the selected period using the new settings. 4. Click “Save”, and the geofence settings are applied. How to view the geofence history In the geofence settings, there is a “Show history” button. Click it to see: The history of all object movements in this zone The date and time of each object s entry and exit The duration of stay in the zone If you want to save the history of movements or events for the geofence, click the “Save to CSV” button.

When the “Geofences” module is connected, a separate “Geofences” tab appears in the object card . On this tab, you can: — link the object to the geofences you need — select the check boxes next to the geofences that should be associated with this object — configure individual parameters for it: idle control, speed control, zone type, alert type Idle control — specify the time in minutes after which staying in the zone is considered idle time. For example, if you specify 15 minutes, the system records an idle period if the object stays in the zone longer than this time. If you specify 0, idle time in this zone is not counted (this is the default value). Speed control — set a speed limit for the object within this geofence. Zone type — choose whether the zone is a working zone or a restricted zone for the object: — working geofence — an area where the object should be and perform its tasks (for example, a warehouse, a construction site, a route) — restricted geofence — an area the object must not enter (for example, private property, hazardous or closed areas, military facilities) Alert type — configure the alert type in this zone: — idle in zone — the system sends an alert if the object stays in the zone longer than the set time — border crossing — the system sends an alert when the object enters or leaves the geofence — idle in zone and border crossing — the system sends an alert on either of these events. After filling in all the parameters, do not forget to click the “Save” button.

A stationary RFID tag can be linked to a geofence. PILOT takes its read into account when determining a visit and records the event even when the object s GPS coordinates are temporarily inaccurate. RFID tag management is available if: — you have administrator rights — the RFID tags module is connected for the account — the geofence belongs to the account and is available for editing How to prepare an RFID tag Before linking, add the RFID tag to the system: 1. Open the “Main” section and go to the “RFID tags” tab 2. Create a new tag or edit an existing one 3. Specify the tag ID. It must match the identifier transmitted by the RFID reader 4. Specify the latitude and longitude. The tag coordinates must be inside the geofence you want to link it to 5. Enable the “Fixed tag” parameter 6. Click “Save” If the tag coordinates are outside the geofence, PILOT does not allow linking. In this case, check the tag coordinates or the geofence boundaries. How to link an RFID tag Open the “Main” section and go to the “Geofences” tab 2. Select the check box next to the geofence you need to display it on the map 3. Make sure the RFID tag is inside the geofence 4. Right-click the geofence and select “Manage RFID tags” 5. Find the tag you need and select it in the link column. To search for a tag by name or identifier, use the “Search” field. To show only the tags already linked to the selected geofence, click “Linked” 6. Click “Save” The RFID tag is linked to the geofence. If the tag coordinates are outside it, PILOT does not allow linking. How a visit is determined When an object detects an RFID tag linked to a geofence, PILOT takes this read into account regardless of the current GPS coordinates. Therefore, a visit can be recorded even if, according to GPS data, the object is outside the geofence. A geofence visit is the period between entry and exit, not each individual tag read. An exit is recorded when both conditions are met: — the object no longer detects the linked RFID tag — according to GPS data, the object is outside the geofence Therefore, several RFID tag reads do not always create several visits. For example, if an object moved away from the tag and then detected it again, but according to GPS stayed inside the geofence all this time, the current visit does not end. How to view tag details on the map Click the RFID tag on the map to open a tooltip. The tooltip shows: the date and time of the last read the tag name the tag identifier coordinates the address The tooltip header shows the object that last detected the RFID tag. If the tag has never been read, there is no object information.

For convenient work with geofences, you can load them into the monitoring system from files or, conversely, save the geofences you created to a file to copy or transfer to other devices. Importing geofences With import, you can add to the system geofences that were created in advance or obtained from other sources. 1. Go to the “Geofences” tab 2. Click the “Import” button 3. Select a KML or KMZ file on your computer KML or KMZ is a special file format for storing geographic data such as points, lines, and areas on a map. 4. Specify the group to load the geofences into 5. Confirm the import — the selected geofences appear in the list and are displayed on the map Exporting geofences Export saves geofences to a file so you can use them in other systems. On the “Geofences” tab, select the check boxes next to the geofences you want to save 2. Click the “Export” button 3. Select the file format — KML or KMZ 4. Specify the group the geofences will be exported from 5. Save the resulting file to your device

Deleting a single zone To delete an unneeded geofence, find it in the list and click the trash icon next to its name. Confirm the deletion, and the zone is removed from the list and no longer displayed on the map. Deleting several zones at once If you want to delete several geofences at once: Hold down the Ctrl key and select all the zones you need in the list. 2. Then right-click the selected zones and click “Delete” 3. Confirm the deletion

Toll roads is a function of the “Geofences” module that accounts for road sections with tolls. Use “Toll roads” to: — control expenses — always know when and how much your objects traveled on toll roads — plan routes — account for tolled sections in advance when building routes — analyze trips — toll road data is saved and available in the report

If the route of a monitoring object includes sections with tolls, you can account for them in the system using the “Toll roads” function. How to create a toll road: 1. Create a geofence of the “Polyline” type Draw on the map the road section that will be tolled. Mark two or more points on the map to build the segment or route you need. 3. Select the “Toll road” check box When creating the zone, select the “Toll road” option so that the system knows this road section is tolled. 3. Configure the line color and width 4. Click “Save” — the toll road appears in the zone list

A special menu is provided for configuring a toll road. Left-click the toll road you need, and you will see the following functions: Gates — configure entry and exit points Scheduler — set conditions and rates for the toll road Delete — delete the toll road How to add toll gates Gates are points on a toll road that record the moment an object enters and exits the tolled section. Thanks to gates, the system determines exactly when an object started and finished driving on the toll road. For accurate accounting of the start and end of the tolled section, add entry and exit points — gates. How to add gates: 1. Open the toll road menu and select “Gates” Click to add a new point 3. Enter the gate name 4. Select the gate type: Entry — marks the place where vehicles enter the toll road Exit — marks the place where vehicles leave the toll road Composite (or complex) — can be both an entry and an exit 5. A gate marker appears on the map. You can move it to the right place. 6. After the gates are added, click “Save”. Depending on the structure of the toll road and the traffic patterns, the system supports different gate configuration options. This lets you account for all trips accurately and correctly calculate the toll for any route. As examples, let us look at two main scenarios: using simple gates and complex gates. Simple gates Simple gates are the option where the entry and exit points are located on the same line (the same section of the toll road). In this case, you simply mark the start and end of the tolled section, and the system records all trips between these two points. For example, a vehicle enters the toll road through “Gate 1” and exits through “Gate 2” on the same section. Even if GPS is temporarily lost on the road (for example, in a tunnel), the system still remembers where the entry and exit were and correctly calculates the toll. Complex gates Complex (or composite) gates are the option where the entry and exit can be on different lines (different sections of toll roads). You can link one line as an entry with another line as an exit, and there can be several such combinations. Such gates are convenient for complex traffic layouts, when a toll road has several routes, interchanges, entries, and exits. They let you account for trips between different sections of toll roads. For example, a vehicle enters the toll road through “Gate A” (on one section) and exits through “Gate B” (on another section). You can create several such links, for example: “Entry 1” — “Exit 1”, “Entry 2” — “Exit 2”, and so on. How to create complex gates: Create toll roads on the map Draw the first section of the toll road on the map as a polyline, set its width, and give it a clear name, for example, Polyline_North. Draw the second section of the toll road and name it, for example, Polyline_South 2. Go to the settings of one of the toll roads, for example, Polyline_North 3. In the toll road menu, select “Gates” 4. Click to add gates 5. Enter the gate name, for example, North_to_South 6. Select the gate type — composite (complex) 7. In the Link zone field, select the second toll road you want to link these gates to, for example, Polyline_South. In the “Location” field, the coordinates are filled in automatically. 8. Click “Save” 9. Configure rates and schedule For this composite pair of gates, you can open the “Scheduler” and set individual rates and a schedule for the route between, for example, Polyline_North and Polyline_South 10. If necessary, create the reverse direction for the second toll road This way, if a vehicle enters the toll road through the gate on Polyline_North and exits through the gate on Polyline_South, the system determines that this is the North_to_South route and applies the corresponding rate and schedule. How to work with the scheduler The scheduler is a tool for configuring the conditions of travel on a toll road. How to configure the scheduler: 1. Open the toll road menu 2. Select “Scheduler” 3. In the “Scheduler” window, configure the parameters Traffic periods: For each day of the week (weekdays, Saturday, Sunday), set the time intervals you need: — normal — high — peak For each period, specify its own time frame, for example, 08:00–10:00 — high traffic. Rates for different vehicle types: For each time period, specify the toll for: — motorcycles and passenger cars — buses and trucks — trucks with trailers Tolerance Click the tolerance button and specify the allowed delay or deviation time so that the system does not treat minor lateness as a violation. 4. After filling in all the parameters, click “Save” at the bottom of the window. The conditions of travel on the toll road are taken into account automatically according to your settings. How to delete a toll road To delete a toll road, open the toll road menu and select “Delete” — after that, the toll road disappears from the zone list and is no longer displayed on the map.

Go to Commands. Click Add. Select one or more devices. Select a template. Specify the command. The Master password is located in the contract s main settings (admin panel). Select a ready-made template or create a new one, then click “Load”. Creating templates for sending commands Click + Click the Create button Specify a name Access rights to templates Use global templates for each language in commands. One of the conditions for commands with configurable parameters is that the parameters are enclosed in percent signs, where n- is a number and s - is a string. Commands for an object Go to the user interface. Open the object s context menu. Select Commands. Select a command. Send it. To view the history, select a period and click the search icon. Admin panel settings 1. Add the module to the account 2. Configure the SMS gateway. Currently, smsgateway24 is supported. You need the device ID and the token from your smsgateway24 subscription: https:// /ax/commands/smsstatus.php?cmd=incoming https:// /ax/commands/smsstatus.php?cmd=status Fill in these parameters in the module configuration section: Template configuration To configure templates: 1. Click the configuration button on the right 2.Open the “Commands” tab. 3.Click the “+” symbol, and a window opens that allows us to edit or add a new command: In this window, we can add a new command, edit the message text, and select in the left panel which vehicles the message will be sent to. 1. When we click the “Send” button, the system sends the message we wrote earlier to the vehicles selected in the left panel. 2. The “Save template” option lets us save the template, which makes it easier to send this command in the future without re-entering the data. When you select this option, the system asks us to give our new template a name: Note: Only an administrator can create templates and assign rights to them to a user, and each template is created for only one device type. Templates must be created for each device type. In the tree, devices are grouped by type: How to load a previously created template? 1. You need to select the devices 2. Select the template you need. 3. Click “Load template” How to delete a command? (available to the administrator only) In the list on the left, we can find the list of previously created templates; just click the icon to delete an unneeded command How to delete a template? (available to the administrator only) After the devices are selected, “Templates” shows us the existing templates, where we can delete one by clicking the icon: User rights to templates To configure user rights to templates, you need to: 1. In the settings, select the “Personnel and groups” button and select the user whose rights you want to configure. 2. The “Edit user” window opens, and we go to the “Commands” option, where we can find the templates and choose which templates this user will have rights to: The “Send command” option By left-clicking a vehicle, we can find the “Send command” option, which lets us see the history of sent messages and also resend messages.

The “Time control” module helps you monitor the working time of vehicles and drivers according to a specified schedule. With it, you can configure: — on which days and hours an object may operate — how long continuous driving is allowed — how long rest should last during the day, at night, and over 24 hours — the maximum time on a route, in a zone, or between zones Based on these settings, the system generates violation notifications — for example, about overwork, insufficient rest, or staying on a route too long. How to configure the working time of an object 1. Go to the “Online” tab 2. Select the object you need in the list 3. Double-click it to open the card 4. In the left panel, select the “Working time” tab The tab consists of several blocks: Days of the week Select the check boxes for the days on which the object may operate Schedule The “Schedule” block sets working intervals by time: Weekdays (Mon–Fri) Saturday Sunday To set the time: 1. Click the icon next to the row you need 2. In the window that opens: Click Specify the working interval If necessary, add several intervals 3. Save the changes Night time The “Night time” block defines the period of the day that is considered night. Specify: — the start time of the night period — the end time of the night period. These settings are used to calculate night rest and generate the corresponding notifications. Alert settings This is where you set the threshold values; when they are exceeded, the system generates notifications. Available parameters: Driving duration (min.) — the allowed time of continuous movement without a break Rest time — day (min.) — the daytime rest standard Rest time — night (min.) — the nighttime rest standard (within the night period) Rest time per 24 hours (min.) — the minimum total rest per 24 hours Max. driving time between zones (min.) — the maximum travel time between geofences Max. parking time in zone (min.) — the maximum allowed parking time in a geofence Max. time on route (min.) — the maximum allowed time on a route from the start to the end of the trip. The object s actual figures are compared with these values. If a violation is recorded, the system can create a notification. How to configure the working time of a driver To work with drivers, the “Drivers” module must be connected. 1. Go to the “Drivers” tab 2. Double-click the driver you need 3. In the card, open the “Working time” tab 4. Configure the schedule: Select the check boxes for the days on which the driver may work In the “Schedule” block, set working intervals by time: Weekdays (Mon–Fri) Saturday Sunday To set the time: 1. Click the icon next to the row you need 2. In the window that opens: Click Specify the working interval 5. Save the changes If you try to assign a driver to a vehicle outside working hours, the system shows a warning and prevents the operation. Default working time settings at the contract level In the admin panel, you can set default working time settings and restrictions for the Time control module at the contract level. These parameters are used as a template: — when adding new objects — for objects that have never had their own settings saved on the “Working time” tab That is, you configure the settings once in the contract — and when an object is created, these values are automatically filled into its card. If necessary, they can be changed at the level of a specific object. You can specify only the parameters you want to make defaults. The remaining fields use system values or are filled in manually. How to specify the configuration 1. Go to the admin panel 2. Open the card of the contract you need 3. Go to the “Module settings” tab 4. Select Time control module 5. In the “Configs” block, add a key and its value, for example, works_day = 1,2,3,4,5 (work from Monday to Friday) max_parking_time = 500 ( no more than 500 minutes of parking in a geofence) max_driving_time = 1000 ( no more than 1000 minutes of driving between geofences) 6. Save the contract settings After that, when a new object is created, the specified parameters automatically appear on the “Working time” tab.
